people.hook: A century before electronic computers existed, Lovelace saw what they would become. Her 1843 notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine contain the first published algorithm written for a machine, and, more radically, the first argument that such machines could work on any symbol, not just numbers. Every general-purpose computer vindicates that insight.
people.name: Ada Lovelace
people.moniker: Pioneer of Computer Programming

people.hook: Aidan Gomez studied mathematics and computer science as an undergraduate at the University of Toronto, working with Roger Grosse, before interning as a student researcher at Google Brain. There, working alongside Jakob Uszkoreit and other Google Brain researchers, he was one of eight co-authors of the 2017 paper Attention Is All You Need, which introduced the Transformer architecture that replaced recurrence and convolution with self-attention and went on to underpin most later large language models. He also co-authored the Reversible Residual Network (RevNet) paper on memory-efficient deep network training. He then pursued doctoral studies in machine learning at the University of Oxford, advised by Yarin Gal and Yee Whye Teh, while leading a research team at the nonprofit lab FOR.ai. In 2019 he co-founded Cohere in Toronto, where as CEO he has helped the company raise close to a billion dollars across four funding rounds and build enterprise-focused large language models.
people.name: Aidan Gomez
people.moniker: Co-founder and CEO, Cohere

people.hook: Turing supplied both of AI's founding documents: the 1936 paper proving one universal machine could compute anything computable, and the 1950 paper asking whether machines can think. The first made computers possible; the second made artificial intelligence a research question rather than a fantasy.
people.name: Alan Turing
people.moniker: Father of Theoretical Computer Science and AI

people.hook: Albert Gu is one of the two authors of Mamba, the 2023 paper that showed a state space model could match Transformer-quality language modeling while scaling linearly instead of quadratically with sequence length. The work built on his earlier S4 research from his Stanford PhD under Chris Re, and it gave the field its first credible architectural alternative to attention. Gu now holds both an academic and a commercial base for that idea, teaching as an Assistant Professor in Carnegie Mellon's Machine Learning Department while serving as Chief Scientist and Co-Founder at Cartesia, a startup applying state space models to real-time voice and audio AI. TIME named him to its 100 Most Influential People in AI in 2024 for that combination of research and applied work.
people.name: Albert Gu
people.moniker: Assistant Professor, Carnegie Mellon University, and Chief Scientist and Co-Founder, Cartesia

people.hook: Alex Krizhevsky was a graduate student in computer science at the University of Toronto, working under Geoffrey Hinton alongside fellow student Ilya Sutskever. In 2012 the three published ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks, describing a large convolutional network, later known as AlexNet, that used GPU training and a new regularization technique to sharply cut image classification error rates. A variant of the network won the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge that year by a wide margin, a result widely credited with convincing the broader field that deep neural networks, trained at scale on GPUs, could outperform earlier computer vision approaches. Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton founded DNNresearch Inc. to build on the work, and in March 2013 Google acquired the company, bringing Krizhevsky and Sutskever onto Google's research staff while Hinton divided his time between Google and the university.
people.name: Alex Krizhevsky
people.moniker: Co-creator of AlexNet

people.hook: Zhavoronkov built Insilico Medicine to prove that generative AI could do more than analyze biology, it could design new drug candidates outright, and Rentosertib, discovered and designed by Insilico's AI pipeline, became one of the first such molecules to reach human clinical trials.
people.name: Alex Zhavoronkov
people.moniker: Pioneer of AI-Driven Drug Discovery

people.hook: Dasdan built his career on the infrastructure layer that makes large-scale data and machine learning systems actually work, from web search ranking research to leading engineering at ad-tech and networking companies, before taking the CTO role at Dropbox as the company reorients its file-storage platform around AI-driven organization and search.
people.name: Ali Dasdan
people.moniker: Data Systems Engineer Turned Dropbox CTO

people.hook: Allen Newell trained as a physicist at Stanford before shifting into mathematics and, after a year at Princeton, joining the RAND Corporation in 1950 to study Air Force logistics and organizational decision making. At RAND he began a long collaboration with Herbert Simon, and in 1955 and 1956 the two of them, working with programmer J.C. Shaw, built the Logic Theorist, a program that could prove theorems from Whitehead and Russell's Principia Mathematica by searching through possible proof steps rather than brute calculation. Newell earned his doctorate at the Carnegie Institute of Technology, where his dissertation grew out of that work, and he joined the Carnegie faculty in 1961, remaining there for the rest of his career. With Simon he went on to build the General Problem Solver, a program meant to capture general human problem solving through means-ends analysis, and the two argued that computers manipulating symbols could serve as a general theory of intelligence, a position they called the physical symbol system hypothesis. In his final years Newell developed Soar, a unified cognitive architecture meant to explain the full range of human cognitive behavior within a single computational framework, and he laid out that ambition in his 1990 book Unified Theories of Cognition. He died of cancer in 1992, shortly after the field had already recognized the sweep of his work through its highest honors.
people.name: Allen Newell
people.moniker: Pioneer of symbolic AI and cognitive architecture

people.hook: Ritualo sits at a position that barely existed five years ago: the combined Chief Data and AI Officer function inside a cabinet-level foreign policy agency. Her career was built entirely on the federal data and performance management side, monitoring and evaluation, division chief, deputy CDAO, making her one of the few senior government AI officers whose path to the role ran through data governance and program evaluation rather than technology procurement.
people.name: Amy Ritualo
people.moniker: Acting Chief Data and AI Officer, U.S. Department of State

people.hook: Germanidis co-founded the generative-video company Runway in 2018 and served as its CTO for over seven years before becoming Co-CEO in 2026. Before Runway he worked in machine learning and computer vision at IBM Research and as a backend engineer at Zocdoc, Chartbeat, and Quantcast.
people.name: Anastasis Germanidis
people.moniker: Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Runway

people.hook: Gilman's brand philosophy, that the best brands make people feel something real, was forged across twenty-five years of payments and fintech marketing where the product is inherently invisible. She helped grow Zelle past a trillion dollars in transactions and launched Paze from scratch to a David Ogilvy Silver Award. Her public view on AI is clear: it is a tool for freeing humans to do what humans do best, and trust, judgment, and creativity remain at the heart of great brands.
people.name: Andrea Gilman
people.moniker: Chief Marketing Officer at Early Warning, Zelle and Paze

people.hook: Andrej Karpathy has spent his career moving between building frontier neural networks and teaching other people how they work. He was a founding research scientist at OpenAI in 2015, then spent five years as Tesla's Director of AI leading the computer vision team behind Autopilot and Full Self-Driving. Along the way he designed and taught CS231n, Stanford's first deep learning course, and built a large public following through blog posts and YouTube lectures that walk through how language models are actually built. After a second stint at OpenAI and a run at his own AI education venture, Eureka Labs, he joined Anthropic's pretraining team in May 2026.
people.name: Andrej Karpathy
people.moniker: AI researcher, Anthropic, and OpenAI co-founder and former Tesla Director of AI

people.hook: Andrew Barto earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics and a PhD in computer and communication sciences, both from the University of Michigan. In 1977 he joined the University of Massachusetts Amherst as a postdoctoral research associate and spent his career there, rising through associate professor and professor to department chair before becoming Professor Emeritus of Information and Computer Sciences. Beginning in the 1980s, working closely with Richard Sutton, he developed the conceptual and algorithmic foundations of reinforcement learning, including temporal difference learning, policy gradient methods and agent designs that combine learning with planning. He and Sutton distilled that work into the textbook Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, first published in 1998 with a second edition in 2018, which became the standard reference for the field. In 2024 the Association for Computing Machinery awarded Barto and Sutton the ACM A.M. Turing Award for this body of work.
people.name: Andrew Barto
people.moniker: Professor Emeritus, University of Massachusetts Amherst

people.hook: Andrew Feldman has built two companies around the same conviction, that general-purpose processors are the wrong tool for specialized workloads. He first proved it with SeaMicro, a microserver startup he founded in 2007 that AMD acquired in 2012 for roughly 334 million dollars. He then co-founded Cerebras Systems in 2015 to apply the same logic to AI, building the Wafer-Scale Engine, a single chip roughly the size of a dinner plate designed specifically to keep AI training data close to compute instead of shuttling it between separate processors. As Cerebras CEO, Feldman has positioned wafer-scale computing as an alternative to clusters of GPUs for large-scale AI training and inference.
people.name: Andrew Feldman
people.moniker: Co-Founder and CEO, Cerebras Systems

people.hook: Ng did more than any single figure to turn machine learning from a graduate-school subject into a skill anyone could learn online, while simultaneously building the industrial-scale infrastructure, Google Brain among it, that made deep learning practical at big-tech scale.
people.name: Andrew Ng
people.moniker: AI Educator and Deep Learning Pioneer

people.hook: Rabinovich arrived at the Longuet-Higgins Prize, the computer vision field's highest honor for work that has stood the test of time, the same year his startup was acquired and he became CTO of a public company. His arc from Google research to Magic Leap's human-centered AR, to founding an AI meeting tool, to leading AI at one of the world's largest freelance platforms is a compressed version of the field's own evolution: from perception research to multimodal generation to enterprise deployment.
people.name: Andrew Rabinovich
people.moniker: CTO and Head of AI at Upwork

people.hook: Yang forced automation and AI's threat to jobs onto the American political stage years before generative AI made the subject unavoidable, building an entire 2020 presidential campaign, and a signature policy proposal, around the argument that AI-driven job loss required a fundamental rethink of the social safety net.
people.name: Andrew Yang
people.moniker: Politician Who Made Automation a National Issue

people.hook: Anima Anandkumar is a computer scientist known for pioneering the use of tensor decomposition methods to give provable guarantees for learning latent variable models, an alternative to techniques that lacked theoretical grounding. She earned a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Technology Madras in 2004 and a PhD in electrical and computer engineering from Cornell University in 2009, followed by a postdoctoral position at MIT. She then built an academic career at the University of California, Irvine, rising from assistant to associate professor, before moving into industry as a principal scientist at Amazon AI and later as director and then senior director of AI research at NVIDIA. Since 2017 she has held the Bren Professorship in Computing and Mathematical Sciences at Caltech, where her group extends foundational machine learning theory into applied problems such as physics informed neural networks, weather forecasting and drug discovery. Her career bridges rigorous theoretical work on learning algorithms with large scale applied AI research built inside major technology companies.
people.name: Anima Anandkumar
people.moniker: Bren Professor of Computing and Mathematical Sciences, Caltech

people.hook: Moisant built his career on the operational spine of technology organizations, infrastructure, security, enterprise platforms, and the internal systems that keep large companies running. At Indeed, overseeing 300 million monthly visitors and three million employers, he sits at the intersection of consumer scale and enterprise risk, leading both the CIO and CSO functions simultaneously.
people.name: Anthony Moisant
people.moniker: CIO and CSO at Indeed

people.hook: Arthur Mensch spent two and a half years researching large language models at Google DeepMind before deciding, alongside longtime friends Guillaume Lample and Timothee Lacroix, that a European lab could compete at the frontier while keeping its models open. The three co-founded Mistral AI in Paris in April 2023, and Mensch has run the company as CEO since, positioning it as an open-weight counterweight to closed labs in the US. He holds a doctorate in machine learning from Paris-Saclay University, following earlier study at Ecole Polytechnique and Telecom Paris, and in 2025 was named a Knight of the French National Order of Merit.
people.name: Arthur Mensch
people.moniker: Co-Founder and CEO, Mistral AI

people.hook: Arthur Samuel trained as an electrical engineer at MIT before spending nearly two decades at Bell Telephone Laboratories working on vacuum tubes and related electronics. After a period teaching at the University of Illinois, he joined IBM in 1949, where he worked on the design of the IBM 701 and 704 computers. In his own time at IBM he wrote a program that played checkers, and rather than encoding a fixed strategy he had it improve through repeated self-play, adjusting its evaluation of board positions based on outcomes and building a memory of positions it had already assessed. He described the work in a 1959 paper in the IBM Journal of Research and Development, using the phrase machine learning to describe a computer's ability to improve at a task without being explicitly reprogrammed for it. Samuel demonstrated an early version of the program on television in 1956, and it stood for years as a widely cited proof that a machine could improve through experience. He moved to Stanford University in 1966, where he continued refining the checkers program and working on computing research until his death in 1990.
people.name: Arthur Samuel
people.moniker: Coined the term machine learning

people.hook: Ashish Vaswani grew up partly in Oman before his family moved to Nagpur, India, when he was fifteen. He earned a bachelor's degree in computer science and engineering from Birla Institute of Technology, Mesra, worked briefly as a computer engineer in Delhi, then completed a master's degree and a PhD in computer science at the University of Southern California. He spent more than six years as a research scientist at Google Brain, and in 2017 he led the eight-author team, including Niki Parmar and Aidan Gomez, that published Attention Is All You Need, introducing the Transformer architecture that replaced recurrence and convolution with self-attention and became the base design for most later large language models. In April 2022 he co-founded Adept AI as chief scientist alongside Niki Parmar and David Luan, before leaving to co-found Essential AI with Parmar, where he now serves as CEO.
people.name: Ashish Vaswani
people.moniker: Co-founder and CEO, Essential AI

people.hook: Bernhard Schölkopf studied physics, mathematics and philosophy in Tübingen and London, then completed a doctorate in computer science at the Technical University of Berlin in 1997. He worked at the German National Research Center for Computer Science and held industrial research posts at AT&T Bell Laboratories, Microsoft Research and Biowulf Technologies, a period in which he helped develop the kernel methods that underlie the support vector machine framework used widely in machine learning. In 2001 he became a director and scientific member at the Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics, and since 2011 he has directed the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems in Tübingen. His research has shifted toward causal machine learning, arguing that statistical learning methods need causal structure to generalize reliably outside their training distribution, work recognized with the 2019 Körber Prize. He also holds an honorary professorship at TU Berlin.
people.name: Bernhard Schölkopf
people.moniker: Director, Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems

people.hook: Sengupta has built enterprise AI functions from scratch at four different organizations, AXA XL, Zebra Technologies, and now JPMorgan Chase, while maintaining an active academic research career that produced over 9,100 citations and a co-authored analysis of the EU AI Act, a rare combination of frontier research credentials and boardroom-level AI deployment experience.
people.name: Biswa Sengupta
people.moniker: Chief AI Technologist and Architect of JPMorgan's LLM Suite

people.hook: Smith turned a $600K loss into an $8 million profit at Piston Group inside a single year, then spent two decades repeating that pattern of operational turnarounds across automotive and manufacturing suppliers ranging from $120 million to over $1 billion in revenue. He now sits on the board of Nikola Motor Company, the autonomous and electric truck maker, while running his own holding company, Voltava.
people.name: Bruce Smith
people.moniker: Owner, Chairman and CEO, Voltava; Nikola Motor Company board member

people.hook: C.C. Wei leads the company that manufactures most of the world's advanced AI chips. He joined TSMC in 1998 after earlier engineering roles at Texas Instruments, ST Microelectronics, and Chartered Semiconductor, and spent the next quarter century rising through business development and operating roles before becoming President and Co-CEO in 2013, sole CEO in 2018, and Chairman and CEO in 2024. Under his leadership TSMC's advanced process nodes have become the manufacturing bottleneck and enabler for the generative AI buildout, supplying the chips behind most leading GPUs and AI accelerators. He holds a PhD in electrical engineering from Yale and has repeatedly told investors that AI-driven demand for TSMC's most advanced capacity remains structurally strong even as supply stays tight.
people.name: C.C. Wei
people.moniker: Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC)

people.hook: Bakalar leads AI ethics at OpenAI after nearly four years as Chief Ethicist at Meta, where she moved from Responsible AI research into leading ethics across GenAI Trust and Safety and Meta Superintelligence Labs. She holds a PhD in Political Science from the University of Pennsylvania and spent seven years on the faculty at Temple University before moving into industry.
people.name: Chloé Bakalar
people.moniker: AI Ethics Lead, OpenAI

people.hook: Chris Olah helped invent the field of mechanistic interpretability, the effort to reverse engineer the internal workings of neural networks into algorithms a person can actually read. He built that career without a college degree, funding it instead with a Thiel Fellowship, then spent years at Google Brain visualizing what neural networks see before leading interpretability research at OpenAI. In 2021 he co-founded Anthropic and now leads its interpretability work, publishing the Transformer Circuits research thread that tries to map language models circuit by circuit. He also co-founded Distill, a journal built around explaining machine learning clearly rather than tersely. In 2026 he took that argument to the Vatican, telling an audience beside Pope Leo XIV that AI's governance problems cannot be left to computer scientists alone.
people.name: Chris Olah
people.moniker: Co-founder and Interpretability Lead, Anthropic

people.hook: Christopher Bishop earned a BA in physics from Oxford University and a PhD in theoretical physics, on quantum field theory, from the University of Edinburgh. He began his research career in fusion plasma physics at the Culham Laboratory, then moved into applied neural computing, heading the Applied Neurocomputing Centre at AEA Technology before taking a chair in the Department of Computer Science and Applied Mathematics at Aston University, where he founded and led the Neural Computing Research Group. He joined Microsoft Research in 1997 and later directed Microsoft Research Cambridge from 2015 to 2022. In 2022 he founded Microsoft Research AI4Science, which he continues to lead. He wrote the widely used textbooks Neural Networks for Pattern Recognition (1995) and Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (2006), and later co-authored Deep Learning: Foundations and Concepts (2024) with his son Hugh Bishop. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 2017.
people.name: Christopher Bishop
people.moniker: Microsoft Technical Fellow, founder of Microsoft Research AI4Science

people.hook: Christopher Ré runs Stanford's Hazy Research lab, which has spent more than a decade turning ideas about data quality and hardware efficiency into companies. His early work on DeepDive, a system for pulling structured facts out of unstructured dark data, won him a MacArthur Fellowship in 2015. He later co-founded Snorkel AI to make labeling training data programmatic instead of manual, and Together AI, alongside collaborators including Tri Dao, Ce Zhang and Percy Liang, to build infrastructure for training and running open foundation models. Along the way his lab's systems work on hardware-aware training has fed directly into how modern language models are trained and served at scale.
people.name: Christopher Ré
people.moniker: Professor of Computer Science, Stanford University, and Founder, Together AI and Snorkel AI

people.hook: Borrowman spent more than a decade inside Colgate-Palmolive's Hill's Pet Nutrition division building global digital marketing systems before moving to the European digital transformation role and then into enterprise AI. Her Davos 2026 appearance placed her in the small cohort of marketing leaders publicly shaping the governance and brand questions that agentic AI raises, specifically, how leadership principles should be embedded directly into AI architecture rather than applied after the fact.
people.name: Christy Borrowman
people.moniker: VP AI Transformation at Colgate-Palmolive

people.hook: Claude Shannon studied electrical engineering and mathematics at the University of Michigan before arriving at MIT, where his 1937 master's thesis showed that Boolean algebra could be used to design and simplify electrical switching circuits, groundwork that digital computer design would later depend on. He earned a PhD in mathematics from MIT in 1940 and spent the years after at Bell Telephone Laboratories, where during the Second World War he worked on fire-control systems and cryptography, producing a classified analysis of secrecy systems that he published openly after the war. In 1948 he published A Mathematical Theory of Communication in the Bell System Technical Journal, defining information mathematically in terms of entropy and showing how much data could reliably be sent over a noisy channel, work that founded information theory and underlies how modern computing represents and transmits information. He returned to MIT as a professor in 1956, continuing his research in communication theory while also experimenting with early electromechanical devices, including a maze-solving device called Theseus that used simple relays to learn a path, an early demonstration of machine memory and adaptive behavior. His concepts of the bit, entropy and channel capacity gave computing a rigorous vocabulary for measuring and manipulating information, an influence that reaches into how artificial intelligence systems handle information and uncertainty. He died in 2001 after some years of declining health.
people.name: Claude Shannon
people.moniker: Founder of information theory

people.hook: Cosoreanu spent nearly two decades rising through GE's energy technology divisions, engineering, program management, and eventually product and CTO roles in grid automation, before taking the CTO seat at GE Vernova as the company builds the grid infrastructure and automation technology the energy transition depends on.
people.name: Claudia Cosoreanu
people.moniker: Chief Technology Officer at GE Vernova

people.hook: Clement Delangue co-founded Hugging Face in 2016 with Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf, originally as a chatbot app, and steered it into the default home for sharing open-source AI models and datasets. Before that he worked in product management at Moodstocks, a computer vision startup that Google acquired the same year Hugging Face began. As CEO he built a platform that by September 2026 hosted more than 3 million models and 500,000 datasets used by more than 18 million developers. That same month he agreed to sell the company to Nvidia for roughly 12.9 billion dollars, negotiating to keep Hugging Face open across clouds, frameworks and chip vendors rather than tied to Nvidia's hardware alone.
people.name: Clement Delangue
people.moniker: Co-founder and CEO, Hugging Face

people.hook: Corinna Cortes earned a masters degree in physics from the University of Copenhagen before completing a PhD in computer science at the University of Rochester in 1993. She joined AT&T Bell Labs in 1989, where she spent more than a decade in the Adaptive Systems Research Group led by Larry Jackel. There she and Vladimir Vapnik developed the soft margin support vector machine, an extension that made support vector machines practical for real world classification problems with noisy, non separable data. Their 1995 paper on support vector networks became one of the most cited papers in machine learning. She later moved to Google, where she founded and now leads Google Research New York as a Vice President, overseeing large scale machine learning research across multiple international teams.
people.name: Corinna Cortes
people.moniker: Vice President, Google Research

people.hook: Dan Hendrycks holds a PhD in computer science from UC Berkeley. In 2016 he and Kevin Gimpel introduced the Gaussian Error Linear Unit (GELU) activation function, which went on to become one of the most widely used activation functions in transformer-based neural networks, including BERT and GPT-style models. In 2020 he led a team that created the MMLU benchmark, a test spanning 57 academic and professional subjects that became a standard way to measure how much large language models actually know rather than how fluently they write. He serves as Executive and Research Director of the Center for AI Safety, a nonprofit focused on reducing societal-scale risks from artificial intelligence, and in 2023 he organized the Statement on AI Risk, a public letter signed by leading AI researchers and company executives that helped push AI extinction risk into mainstream policy debate. He also advises xAI and Scale AI and wrote the textbook Introduction to AI Safety, Ethics, and Society.
people.name: Dan Hendrycks
people.moniker: Executive Director, Center for AI Safety

people.hook: Daniela Amodei runs the day-to-day operations of Anthropic, the AI safety company she co-founded with her brother Dario in 2021 after both left OpenAI. Her path there ran through Capitol Hill and international development work before she spent years at Stripe, helping grow the company from about 40 employees to more than 300 and later working on platform risk with engineers, ML specialists and lawyers. At OpenAI she focused on AI safety and policy before deciding to help start a company built around that idea from the ground up. As President, she describes her job as taking the technical safety vision of Anthropic's research leadership and turning it into concrete operating norms for the company.
people.name: Daniela Amodei
people.moniker: Co-founder and President, Anthropic

people.hook: Daphne Koller earned undergraduate and masters degrees in computer science from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem before completing a PhD in computer science at Stanford University in 1993. She joined the Stanford faculty in 1995 and spent nearly two decades there as the Rajeev Motwani Professor of Computer Science, building a research program in probabilistic graphical models, a framework for reasoning under uncertainty that she detailed with Nir Friedman in the widely used textbook Probabilistic Graphical Models, Principles and Techniques. In 2012 she co-founded Coursera with fellow Stanford professor Andrew Ng, serving as co-CEO and president as the platform grew into one of the largest providers of massive open online courses. She later served as chief computing officer at Calico, an Alphabet company focused on aging research, before founding insitro in 2018, where she is CEO and applies machine learning and large scale biological data to drug discovery and development.
people.name: Daphne Koller
people.moniker: Founder and CEO, insitro, co-founder of Coursera

people.hook: Dario Amodei trained as a physicist, earning a Ph.D. in biophysics from Princeton as a Hertz Fellow before moving into machine learning at Baidu, briefly at Google Brain, and then at OpenAI. As OpenAI's Vice President of Research, he set research direction, led the teams that built GPT-2 and GPT-3, and helped pioneer reinforcement learning from human feedback. In 2021 he left to co-found Anthropic, where as CEO he has pushed the idea that AI safety and frontier capability can be built together rather than traded off. He argues that case publicly too, from his 2024 essay Machines of Loving Grace on AI's potential upside to a 2025 New York Times op-ed calling for basic transparency rules on frontier AI development.
people.name: Dario Amodei
people.moniker: Co-founder and CEO, Anthropic

people.hook: David Holz built the generative image tool that made AI art a mainstream habit. Before Midjourney, he spent more than a decade as co-founder and CTO of Leap Motion, developing hand-tracking hardware that never found its mass market. He founded Midjourney in 2021 as an independent research lab, kept it privately held, and grew it past 20 million users without taking outside investment. He describes the project as an attempt to expand human imagination rather than to build imaginative machines, and Disney and Universal's 2025 copyright lawsuit against the company shows how far that project now reaches into the rest of the entertainment industry.
people.name: David Holz
people.moniker: Founder, Midjourney

people.hook: David Rumelhart earned a bachelors degree in psychology and mathematics from the University of South Dakota before completing a PhD in mathematical psychology at Stanford University in 1967. He then joined the faculty at the University of California, San Diego, where he helped build the Parallel Distributed Processing research group that modeled cognition as patterns of activity distributed across networks of simple units. With Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams, he co-authored the 1986 Nature paper Learning Representations by Back Propagating Errors, which showed how multilayer neural networks could be trained efficiently and became one of the founding texts of modern deep learning. That same year he and James McClelland published the two volume Parallel Distributed Processing, Explorations in the Microstructure of Cognition, which brought connectionist ideas to a wide audience of psychologists, neuroscientists and computer scientists. He returned to Stanford as a professor in 1987, continuing his work in cognitive science until a neurodegenerative illness ended his research career in the late 1990s. He died in Chelsea, Michigan, on March 13, 2011, at the age of 68.
people.name: David Rumelhart
people.moniker: Cognitive scientist, co-inventor of backpropagation

people.hook: Sachdeva built a career converting large-scale corporate transactions, over $11 billion of them, into working technology systems, from integrating GE's manufacturing ERPs to modernizing Sabre's airline cloud infrastructure, before bringing that private-sector integration discipline to the U.S. Air Force as its Chief Information Officer.
people.name: Deepak Sachdeva
people.moniker: Chief Information Officer, United States Air Force

people.hook: Demis Hassabis showed an early talent for chess, reaching master strength as a teenager, before studying computer science at Cambridge and going on to design the video game Theme Park and lead AI programming on Black and White at Lionhead Studios. After running his own studio, Elixir Studios, he returned to academia and earned a PhD in cognitive neuroscience from University College London in 2009, studying memory and imagination. In 2010 he co-founded DeepMind with Shane Legg and Mustafa Suleyman to pursue general purpose learning systems, and Google acquired the company in 2014. Under his leadership DeepMind built landmark reinforcement learning systems, including AlphaGo, which defeated Go world champion Lee Sedol in 2016, and AlphaFold, which predicts the three dimensional structure of proteins from their amino acid sequences. Following a 2023 merger with Google Brain, he now leads the combined organization as co-founder and CEO of Google DeepMind. In 2024 he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, shared with John Jumper and David Baker, for work on protein structure prediction, and was knighted for services to artificial intelligence.
people.name: Demis Hassabis
people.moniker: Co-founder and CEO, Google DeepMind

people.hook: Dolgov has been inside Google and Waymo's self-driving effort from its earliest days as a Google X project through its emergence as the first company to operate paid, fully driverless rides at commercial scale, rising from founding engineer to Co-CEO across that entire arc.
people.name: Dmitri Dolgov
people.moniker: Co-CEO Who Took Waymo Driverless

people.hook: Donald Hebb trained first in English literature at Dalhousie University before turning to psychology, earning a master's degree at McGill University and then a PhD at Harvard under Karl Lashley, whose research on the brain's role in learning shaped Hebb's own direction. After periods at Queen's University and the Yerkes Laboratories of Primate Biology, he joined McGill University in 1947, where he spent the rest of his career and eventually chaired the psychology department. In 1949 he published The Organization of Behavior: A Neuropsychological Theory, proposing that learning and memory arise physically in the brain when one neuron's repeated activity helps fire another, strengthening the connection between them, a mechanism now known as Hebbian learning or Hebb's postulate. That idea gave later researchers a concrete, biologically grounded rule for how neural connections might change with experience, and it became a founding principle for artificial neural network models, from Frank Rosenblatt's Perceptron through much later connectionist research. Hebb also developed the Hebb-Williams maze for testing animal intelligence and studied how early experience and sensory deprivation shape later behavior. He remained closely tied to McGill until his death in 1985, having also served as the university's chancellor.
people.name: Donald Hebb
people.moniker: Founder of Hebbian learning theory

people.hook: Edward Feigenbaum studied electrical engineering at the Carnegie Institute of Technology, where he also earned his PhD under Herbert Simon, building EPAM, an early computer model of human memory and learning. He joined the faculty at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1960 and moved to Stanford University in 1965, where he spent most of his career and later chaired the computer science department. At Stanford he worked with the geneticist Joshua Lederberg on DENDRAL, a program that inferred the molecular structure of chemical compounds from mass spectrometry data by encoding the reasoning of expert chemists, widely regarded as the first true expert system. Feigenbaum and his colleagues went on to build MYCIN, a program that used a similar rule-based approach to help diagnose bacterial infections and recommend antibiotic treatment, and his work established knowledge engineering, the practice of capturing human expertise as computable rules, as a distinct discipline within artificial intelligence. He directed Stanford's Knowledge Systems Laboratory for many years, served as chief scientist of the United States Air Force from 1994 to 1997, and in 1994 shared the A.M. Turing Award with Raj Reddy for demonstrating the practical and commercial potential of large-scale artificial intelligence systems.
people.name: Edward Feigenbaum
people.moniker: Pioneer of expert systems

people.hook: Eliezer Yudkowsky is an American writer and researcher who has spent more than two decades arguing that artificial intelligence poses a serious risk to humanity's survival. Without a formal academic degree, he co-founded the Singularity Institute for Artificial Intelligence, later renamed the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, with Brian and Sabine Atkins in 2000 to help accelerate the arrival of smarter than human AI. Within a few years he concluded that building such systems safely was a harder and more urgent problem than building them at all, and he redirected the institute's research toward what became known as AI alignment. Between 2006 and 2012 he wrote a long series of essays on rationality, cognitive bias, and AI risk that helped found the online community LessWrong and were later collected into the book Rationality: From AI to Zombies. In 2023 he argued in a Time magazine essay that a temporary pause on AI development was not enough and called for governments to shut down large AI training runs entirely. In 2025 he co-authored If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies with fellow MIRI researcher Nate Soares, bringing his warnings about superintelligent AI to a mainstream audience.
people.name: Eliezer Yudkowsky
people.moniker: AI alignment researcher and co-founder of MIRI

people.hook: Emad Mostaque founded Stability AI in 2019 and turned it into the company behind Stable Diffusion, the open-weight image model that pushed generative AI into public use in August 2022. A former hedge fund manager, he positioned Stability AI as a counterweight to closed AI labs, backing open releases rather than gating models behind an API. He resigned as CEO and left the board in March 2024, saying he wanted to pursue decentralized AI outside a single company, and by late 2024 Stability AI confirmed he no longer had any control over it.
people.name: Emad Mostaque
people.moniker: Founder, Stability AI

people.hook: Nguyen holds a Stanford PhD combining AI with bioengineering and spent years on deepfake detection at Facebook AI and Adobe before research internships in Fei-Fei Li's and Leonidas Guibas's labs and at Google DeepMind's co-scientist team. He now leads Radical Numerics, a company he co-founded to build what he describes as general biological intelligence.
people.name: Eric Nguyen
people.moniker: Co-Founder and CEO, Radical Numerics

people.hook: Brynjolfsson has spent three decades building the empirical case for how digital technology, and now AI, actually changes productivity and jobs, work that shifted from academic papers to boardroom strategy as generative AI forced every company to ask the same question he had been measuring for years.
people.name: Erik Brynjolfsson
people.moniker: Economist of the Second Machine Age

people.hook: Li made modern AI's breakthrough possible by betting on data before it was fashionable: ImageNet's fourteen million labeled images gave the field the benchmark on which AlexNet proved deep learning worked. She has spent the years since insisting the technology stay pointed at people, building Stanford HAI and carrying the human-centered case into policy rooms from Sacramento to Washington.
people.name: Fei-Fei Li
people.moniker: The Godmother of AI

people.hook: Frank Rosenblatt studied psychology at Cornell University, earning his PhD there in 1956, and went to work at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory in Buffalo, New York, where he began developing a mathematical model of how the brain might learn to recognize patterns. In 1957 and 1958 he built the Perceptron, a network of simple, adjustable units loosely modeled on neurons, and described it in a 1958 paper as a probabilistic model for information storage and pattern recognition in the brain. With funding from the Office of Naval Research, he and his collaborators built a physical version called the Mark I Perceptron, using potentiometers to represent adjustable connection weights and motors to carry out the learning process, and it could learn to distinguish simple visual patterns after being shown examples. The 1958 unveiling drew wide press coverage and considerable hype about the machine's potential, though the model's practical limitations, later highlighted in Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert's 1969 book Perceptrons, contributed to a broader cooling of interest in neural network research for years afterward. Rosenblatt later became a professor at Cornell University in Ithaca, working in brain and behavioral sciences and continuing to study perceptron-like models until his death in a boating accident on Chesapeake Bay in 1971. Decades later the layered, adjustable-weight structure he pioneered became the basis for the neural networks used throughout modern artificial intelligence, and the Smithsonian now holds the original Mark I Perceptron in its collection.
people.name: Frank Rosenblatt
people.moniker: Inventor of the Perceptron

people.hook: Bell moved from theoretical chemistry research at Berkeley and Caltech into technology leadership at Uber, then led data science and AI organizations across four different industries, energy at bp, automotive at Ford, and now retail at The Home Depot, one of the few executives to have run enterprise AI at that scale in more than one sector.
people.name: Franziska Bell
people.moniker: CTO of The Home Depot, Four-Industry Technology Executive

people.hook: François Chollet created Keras, the deep learning library that became a default entry point into neural networks for millions of developers, while working as a Google engineer for close to a decade. In 2019 he published the ARC-AGI benchmark, arguing that measuring intelligence required tasks a system could not memorize its way through, and in 2024 he put a million dollars behind a public prize to beat it. He left Google in November 2024 to co-found Ndea with former Zapier president Mike Knoop, betting that program synthesis rather than further scaling is the more promising path toward general AI systems.
people.name: François Chollet
people.moniker: Co-founder, Ndea

people.hook: Hinton kept faith with neural networks through two AI winters, and won. The training method he championed in 1986 and the 2012 breakthrough his lab produced turned a marginal idea into the technology behind modern AI. Then, at the peak of vindication, he quit Google to warn the world about what he had helped build, giving AI risk its most credentialed voice.
people.name: Geoffrey Hinton
people.moniker: The Godfather of Deep Learning

people.hook: Georgi Gerganov changed how large language models reach ordinary computers. Working from Sofia, Bulgaria, he built the ggml tensor library and then llama.cpp, a C and C++ inference engine that let Meta's LLaMA models run on a laptop through aggressive quantization instead of a data-center GPU. He founded ggml.ai in 2023 on pre-seed funding from Nat Friedman and Daniel Gross to sustain the project, and in February 2026 he and his team joined Hugging Face so llama.cpp would have long-term backing while staying fully open source.
people.name: Georgi Gerganov
people.moniker: Creator, ggml and llama.cpp

people.hook: Greg Brockman helped write OpenAI's founding announcement in December 2015 and has run its engineering effort ever since, first as chief technology officer and then, from November 2023, as president. Before that he left MIT to join Stripe in its earliest days, when the payments company was still called dev slash payments, and stayed through its rise into a major engineering organization as chief technology officer. He testified to the Senate about AI policy as early as November 2016, years before the topic reached the mainstream, and he was reinstated as OpenAI's president within days of the company's November 2023 board crisis.
people.name: Greg Brockman
people.moniker: President and Co-founder, OpenAI

people.hook: Guillaume Lample spent his early career at Facebook AI Research pushing multilingual natural language processing forward, then helped build the LLaMA models that reshaped the open-weight AI race. In April 2023 he left Meta to co-found Mistral AI with Arthur Mensch and Timothee Lacroix, taking the role of Chief Scientist. Within two months the young company had raised a European-record seed round, and within six months it had shipped an open-weight model that rivals judged competitive with far larger closed systems. He remains the technical architect behind Mistral's model line, from the first 7B release through its largest frontier models.
people.name: Guillaume Lample
people.moniker: Co-founder and Chief Scientist, Mistral AI

people.hook: Herbert Simon entered the University of Chicago in 1933 hoping to become what he called a mathematical social scientist, studying under mentors including the logician Rudolf Carnap and political scientist Charles Merriam. After finishing his undergraduate degree in 1936 and later a PhD, he built a career studying how organizations and individuals actually make decisions under limits of time, knowledge and computing power, a theory he called bounded rationality. In 1949 he joined the Carnegie Institute of Technology, now Carnegie Mellon University, to help build its Graduate School of Industrial Administration around economics and behavioral science. Around 1954 he began working with Allen Newell to use computer simulation to study human problem solving, and together with Cliff Shaw they built the Logic Theorist in 1956, widely considered the first program designed to mimic human reasoning, followed by the more general General Problem Solver in 1957. Simon spent the rest of his career at Carnegie Mellon studying cognition, organizations and artificial intelligence, work recognized with the 1975 ACM Turing Award, shared with Newell, and the 1978 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for his research on decision making in economic organizations.
people.name: Herbert Simon
people.moniker: Nobel laureate who founded artificial intelligence alongside Allen Newell

people.hook: Ian Goodfellow studied computer science at Stanford University, earning undergraduate and masters degrees while working with Andrew Ng, before completing a PhD in machine learning at the Universite de Montreal in 2015 under Yoshua Bengio and Aaron Courville. While a graduate student he devised Generative Adversarial Networks, a framework in which two neural networks, a generator and a discriminator, are trained against each other so the generator learns to produce increasingly realistic data. He and his coauthors described the idea in a 2014 paper that became one of the most influential works in deep learning and gave rise to a large body of research on image synthesis and generative modeling. After completing his PhD he continued this line of research at OpenAI, contributing to work on improving the stability of GAN training. He also co-authored the widely used textbook Deep Learning with Bengio and Courville, published by MIT Press in 2016.
people.name: Ian Goodfellow
people.moniker: Inventor of Generative Adversarial Networks

people.hook: Illia Polosukhin worked as a machine learning engineer at Google, where he contributed to high level APIs for TensorFlow and worked on question answering systems used in Google Search. In 2017 he was one of eight coauthors of the paper Attention Is All You Need, which introduced the Transformer architecture built entirely on attention mechanisms and became the foundation for the large language models that followed. The next year he left Google and, together with Alexander Skidanov and other collaborators, began building a new blockchain protocol out of a small office in San Francisco. That project became NEAR Protocol, a sharded, proof of stake blockchain designed for usability and scalability, which launched its mainnet in 2020. Polosukhin continues to serve as a co-founder of NEAR, and has more recently worked on bringing large language model and AI agent technology into the NEAR ecosystem.
people.name: Illia Polosukhin
people.moniker: Co-founder, NEAR Protocol

people.hook: Ilya Sutskever was born in Nizhny Novgorod, Russia, and moved with his family first to Israel and then to Canada, where he studied computer science at the University of Toronto under Geoffrey Hinton. In 2012 he co-authored the AlexNet paper with Alex Krizhevsky and Hinton, a deep convolutional network that sharply cut ImageNet classification error rates and helped launch the modern deep learning era. He followed this in 2014 with Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks, showing that a general encoder-decoder architecture could handle tasks like machine translation. In December 2015 he co-founded OpenAI, serving first as Research Director and later as Chief Scientist while the lab built its GPT model series. He left OpenAI in 2024 and co-founded Safe Superintelligence Inc with Daniel Gross and Daniel Levy, a company dedicated to a single goal, building safe superintelligence, and became its CEO in mid-2025 after Gross departed.
people.name: Ilya Sutskever
people.moniker: Co-founder and CEO, Safe Superintelligence Inc.

people.hook: Suh spent over 23 years at IBM, rising to head global strategic partnerships worth more than $10 billion before leading Watson AI product units in commerce, supply chain and collaboration; she then served as President of DocuSign and on its board through its 2018 IPO before becoming CEO of Niantic Spatial, a company building real-world foundation models for physical AI.
people.name: Inhi Cho Suh
people.moniker: CEO, Niantic Spatial

people.hook: J.C.R. Licklider trained as an experimental psychologist, earning his PhD at the University of Rochester before working on psychoacoustics at Harvard during the Second World War. He later moved into engineering circles at MIT, where hands-on exposure to early computers convinced him that machines could become active partners in human thought rather than passive calculators. In 1957 he ran a self study tracking his own workday and found that most of his time went to mechanical tasks that stood between him and actual thinking, an observation that fed directly into his influential 1960 paper Man-Computer Symbiosis, which argued that people and computers should work together in close, real time partnership. In 1962 he became the first director of the Information Processing Techniques Office at the Advanced Research Projects Agency, where he funded university computer science research across the country and, in an internal 1963 memo, sketched an early vision of computers linked together into what he called an intergalactic network. That funding program and the community of researchers it supported helped lay the intellectual groundwork that led to the ARPANET later in the decade.
people.name: J.C.R. Licklider
people.moniker: Psychologist who envisioned human-computer symbiosis and funded the roots of the internet

people.hook: Mineart began as a mechanical engineer at Caterpillar in 1999 and spent nearly three decades rising through engineering, product strategy, and electric power leadership roles before being named Chief Technology Officer, now leading Cat Technology's push to integrate smarter, more connected machines across Caterpillar's global equipment lines.
people.name: Jaime Mineart
people.moniker: Chief Technology Officer of Caterpillar

people.hook: Jakob Uszkoreit grew up in Saarbrücken, Germany, and studied computer science and mathematics at the Berlin Institute of Technology, completing his master's degree summa cum laude in 2008. He joined Google that year after an earlier research internship, working first on data mining for Google Translate and later leading a semantic parsing team supporting Google Search and Assistant. In 2017 he co-authored Attention Is All You Need with colleagues at Google Brain, introducing the Transformer architecture that replaced recurrence and convolution with self-attention and became the foundation for most large language models built since. In 2021 he left Google to co-found Inceptive with biochemist Rhiju Das, applying deep learning models to the design of RNA-based medicines and pairing computational predictions with laboratory testing.
people.name: Jakob Uszkoreit
people.moniker: Co-founder and CEO, Inceptive

people.hook: Jakub Pachocki joined OpenAI in 2017 as a theoretical computer scientist fresh from a PhD in convex optimization, and rose to run the research programs behind some of the company's largest bets, including GPT-4 and the reinforcement-learning system that beat the world Dota 2 champions. In May 2024 OpenAI named him Chief Scientist, succeeding Ilya Sutskever, putting him in charge of the company's core research direction. He is credited with helping steer OpenAI toward reasoning models that work through problems step by step, an approach that produced systems scoring at gold-medal level on the International Mathematical Olympiad. Sam Altman has called him one of the strongest research minds at the company.
people.name: Jakub Pachocki
people.moniker: Chief Scientist, OpenAI

people.hook: Jared Kaplan built his early career as a theoretical physicist, holding a PhD from Harvard and a faculty position at Johns Hopkins studying quantum gravity and conformal field theory. Starting in 2018 he turned that background toward machine learning, working on how language model performance scales with compute, data and parameters, research his own university describes as feeding into GPT-3. In 2021 he co-founded Anthropic and became its Chief Science Officer, leading the technical research behind models like Claude and methods such as Constitutional AI. He still holds his Johns Hopkins physics appointment alongside his role at Anthropic.
people.name: Jared Kaplan
people.moniker: Co-founder and Chief Science Officer, Anthropic

people.hook: Patel has run product at four different points along enterprise software's evolution, content management at Doculabs, cloud file sync at EMC and Syncplicity, cloud content at Box, and now security, collaboration, and AI infrastructure at Cisco, rising to President and Chief Product Officer as the company repositions its networking core around AI.
people.name: Jeetu Patel
people.moniker: President and Chief Product Officer at Cisco

people.hook: Jeff Dean earned a bachelor's degree in computer science and economics from the University of Minnesota in 1990 and a PhD in computer science from the University of Washington in 1996, then worked at Digital Equipment Corporation before joining Google in 1999. At Google he co-designed MapReduce with Sanjay Ghemawat in 2004 and Bigtable in 2006, two systems that became core infrastructure for processing and storing data at massive scale. In 2011 he co-founded the Google Brain team, and in 2015 he helped design and open source TensorFlow, one of the most widely used machine learning frameworks. He also pushed Google to build custom AI accelerator chips, leading to multiple generations of Tensor Processing Units, and now serves as Chief Scientist for Google Research and Google DeepMind, helping set the company's AI research direction.
people.name: Jeff Dean
people.moniker: Chief Scientist, Google Research and Google DeepMind

people.hook: Jensen Huang founded NVIDIA in 1993 and has run it continuously ever since, first as a graphics chip maker for PC gaming and later as the dominant supplier of the GPUs that power modern AI training and inference. He holds a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from Oregon State University and a master's from Stanford, and worked at LSI Logic and Advanced Micro Devices before starting NVIDIA. Under his leadership the company introduced the GPU in 1999, a product line that eventually became the core infrastructure of the generative AI boom. He has since been recognized with engineering's biggest honors, including a share of the 2025 Queen Elizabeth Prize for Engineering and the 2026 IEEE Medal of Honor.
people.name: Jensen Huang
people.moniker: Founder, President and CEO, NVIDIA

people.hook: Jerome Friedman trained as a physicist, earning a PhD from the University of California, Berkeley before working as a research physicist in high-energy physics. In 1972 he joined the Stanford Computation Research Group, and in 1982 he was appointed a professor of statistics at Stanford University. With Leo Breiman, Richard Olshen and Charles Stone he co-developed Classification and Regression Trees (CART), published in 1984, and in 1991 he introduced Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines (MARS) in the Annals of Statistics. In 2001 he published Greedy Function Approximation, formalizing gradient boosting machines as a general method that later became central to widely used tools for structured data prediction. He also co-authored the textbook The Elements of Statistical Learning with Trevor Hastie and Robert Tibshirani, and is now Professor of Statistics, Emeritus, at Stanford.
people.name: Jerome Friedman
people.moniker: Professor of Statistics, Emeritus, Stanford University

people.hook: Fowler ran technology for one of America's largest industrial conglomerates, GE, where he oversaw a $3 billion budget and 25,000 employees and drove the insourcing of thousands of technology jobs, before leading Nationwide's digital transformation and now shaping Lumen's AI-driven network strategy as its CTPO.
people.name: Jim Fowler
people.moniker: Chief Technology and Product Officer at Lumen Technologies

people.hook: Jim Keller has spent four decades moving between the biggest names in semiconductors, leaving a distinct architecture behind at each stop. He led design of AMD's Zen microarchitecture, the chip line credited with reviving the company's competitiveness against Intel, and earlier led the engineering behind Apple's A4 and A5 mobile processors after Apple acquired P.A. Semi. He later ran Autopilot hardware engineering at Tesla and Silicon Engineering at Intel before moving into AI accelerator chips. He is now CEO of Tenstorrent and has also co-founded Atomic Semi, a startup building small-scale chip fabs.
people.name: Jim Keller
people.moniker: CEO, Tenstorrent

people.hook: John McCarthy earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics from Caltech in 1948 and a PhD in mathematics from Princeton in 1951. In August 1955, together with Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon, he wrote the proposal for a summer research project at Dartmouth College built on the idea that every aspect of learning or intelligence could in principle be described precisely enough for a machine to simulate it, a document that introduced the field's name. The 1956 Dartmouth workshop that followed brought together many of the researchers who would go on to define artificial intelligence as a discipline. While at MIT in 1958, McCarthy created the Lisp programming language, which became the dominant tool for AI research for decades because of its ability to manipulate symbolic expressions. He moved to Stanford University in 1962, where he founded the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory and continued developing logic based approaches to reasoning and knowledge representation until his retirement in 2000.
people.name: John McCarthy
people.moniker: Coined the term artificial intelligence and created the Lisp programming language

people.hook: Whyte became CEO of the American Medical Association in 2025 after nearly seven years as Chief Medical Officer of WebMD, and earlier spent nearly five years at the FDA and over eight years as chief medical expert at Discovery Channel. He holds an MD and an MPH from Harvard.
people.name: John Whyte
people.moniker: CEO, American Medical Association

people.hook: Jonathan Ross started what became Google's Tensor Processing Unit as an internal side project, then left to found Groq in 2016, building a chip architecture designed purely for AI inference. Groq's language processing units made the company one of the most closely watched hardware challengers to Nvidia. In December 2025 Nvidia took a non-exclusive license to Groq's technology and hired Ross along with most of Groq's engineering team, a deal that returned billions of dollars to Groq's shareholders and moved its founder inside the company his chips were built to compete with. Ross now works at Nvidia as its chief software architect, and has spoken candidly about the leadership mistakes he made running Groq for nearly a decade.
people.name: Jonathan Ross
people.moniker: Chief Software Architect at Nvidia, founder of Groq

people.hook: Reis-Filho built his career deciphering cancer genomics at the bench, at the Institute of Cancer Research and then as Chief of Experimental Pathology at Memorial Sloan Kettering, before moving to AstraZeneca to apply AI foundation models and agentic frameworks directly to drug discovery and clinical development, one of the clearer examples of a working oncologist becoming an enterprise AI leader.
people.name: Jorge Reis-Filho
people.moniker: Chief of AI for Science Innovation at AstraZeneca

people.hook: Joy Buolamwini is a computer scientist whose research exposed how commercial facial recognition systems perform far worse on darker skinned faces than lighter skinned ones. While a graduate researcher at the MIT Media Lab, she found that some facial analysis software failed to detect her own face until she put on a white mask, an experience that led her to start systematically testing commercial systems for bias. In 2016 she founded the Algorithmic Justice League to combine research, art, and advocacy against harmful bias in AI systems. Her 2018 study Gender Shades, co-authored with Timnit Gebru, tested facial analysis products from IBM, Microsoft, and Face++ using a new benchmark built from images of parliamentarians in African and European countries, and found error rates for darker skinned women far higher than for lighter skinned men. She holds a bachelor's degree in computer science from the Georgia Institute of Technology, studied at Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar, and earned her PhD from the MIT Media Lab. Her work has since informed congressional testimony on facial recognition technology, the 2020 documentary Coded Bias, and her 2023 book Unmasking AI.
people.name: Joy Buolamwini
people.moniker: Computer scientist and founder of the Algorithmic Justice League

people.hook: Judea Pearl earned a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from the Technion in Israel in 1960, then went on to complete master's degrees in electronics and physics in the United States before earning a PhD in electrical engineering from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn in 1965. He joined the computer science faculty at UCLA in 1969 and later founded its Cognitive Systems Laboratory. In the 1980s Pearl developed Bayesian networks, a mathematical framework for representing and reasoning about uncertain relationships among many variables, set out in his 1988 monograph Probabilistic Reasoning in Intelligent Systems, which reshaped how artificial intelligence systems handle uncertainty. He then turned to an even harder problem, building a formal calculus, including what he called the do-calculus, for distinguishing genuine causation from mere correlation using data, work collected in his 2000 book Causality. He later explained these ideas for a general audience in The Book of Why, published in 2018. For this body of work he received the ACM A.M. Turing Award in 2011.
people.name: Judea Pearl
people.moniker: Creator of Bayesian networks and the modern mathematics of causal reasoning

people.hook: Julien Chaumond co-founded Hugging Face in 2016 and has served as its chief technology officer since, building the technical infrastructure, the Hub, the Transformers library, and the huggingface_hub client, that turned the company into the default distribution point for open machine learning models. Before Hugging Face he ran two earlier startups, Prodcast and the reading platform Glose, and advised the French Deputy Minister for Digital Affairs. He describes Hugging Face's approach as belonging to its user community rather than standing apart from it, a framing that has shaped the company's open-source strategy as its Hub scaled to millions of hosted models and datasets.
people.name: Julien Chaumond
people.moniker: Co-founder and Chief Technology Officer, Hugging Face

people.hook: Jürgen Schmidhuber was born in Munich, Germany, and earned his doctorate in computer science from the Technical University of Munich in 1991. In 1990 he proposed an early adversarial training scheme in which two neural networks competed against each other, an idea later recognized as anticipating generative adversarial networks. In 1997 he and his student Sepp Hochreiter published Long Short-Term Memory, a recurrent neural network architecture that overcame the vanishing gradient problem and became one of the most widely used designs in speech recognition and language modeling before the rise of Transformers. He has long served as Scientific Director of the Swiss AI Lab IDSIA, and since 2021 has also directed the AI Initiative at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology. He co-founded NNAISENSE, a company applying his lab's neural network research to industrial and robotic systems.
people.name: Jürgen Schmidhuber
people.moniker: Scientific Director, Swiss AI Lab IDSIA

people.hook: Krithivasan runs the largest IT services company in India and one of the largest in the world, and in September 2026 put its name on the largest AI data centre campus the country has announced: a 1 gigawatt, 250-acre, Rs 70,000 crore project in Hyderabad through the TCS subsidiary HyperVault. He reached the top of TCS after thirty-four years inside it, most of them running the banking, financial services and insurance business that is the company's biggest vertical. His stated programme as chief executive has been to build what TCS calls the world's largest AI-ready workforce, and the Hyderabad campus is the infrastructure side of that same claim.
people.name: K. Krithivasan
people.moniker: CEO and Managing Director, Tata Consultancy Services

people.hook: Dixon became Chancellor of North Carolina Central University in 2024 after leading Elizabeth City State University for over eight years, including as interim and then permanent Chancellor, and after six years overseeing academic and student affairs system-wide for the 17-campus University of North Carolina system. Her research has focused on college access and summer bridge programs.
people.name: Karrie G. Dixon
people.moniker: Chancellor, North Carolina Central University

people.hook: Shankel built her career in the operational and technical backbone of the automotive industry, general management, manufacturing processes, market expansion, before moving into the CTO seat at a commercial vehicle manufacturer and then founding her own technology company. Her PhD in organizational leadership combined with hands-on OEM manufacturing experience places her at the intersection of people-driven transformation and industrial technology adoption.
people.name: Kelleigh Shankel
people.moniker: CEO of Limelight Logic

people.hook: Milchanowski built her career at the intersection of AI and financial crime, from model risk management at JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley to leading a global AI and quantum lab at EY that supported the U.S. National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence, before becoming BMO's first Chief AI and Quantum Officer and founding director of its applied AI institute.
people.name: Kristin Milchanowski
people.moniker: Chief AI and Quantum Officer at BMO Financial Group

people.hook: Morgan's career is a direct map of where AI governance is coming from in media and entertainment: she built operational legal structures for emerging digital platforms, streaming, apps, immersive venues, before the AI inflection point arrived, then moved into AI legal strategy at Amazon and NBCUniversal. The frameworks she builds now govern how a company the size of NBCU evaluates, procures, and deploys AI across its entire enterprise.
people.name: Lasherelle Morgan
people.moniker: SVP, Legal AI Innovation at NBCUniversal

people.hook: Leo Breiman earned a physics degree from Caltech in 1949, a master's degree in mathematics from Columbia in 1950, and a PhD from UC Berkeley in 1954, after which he taught probability theory at UCLA. He later resigned his tenured position to spend more than a decade as an independent statistical consultant, working on problems like traffic pattern and ozone level prediction, before joining the UC Berkeley Department of Statistics faculty in 1980. With Jerome Friedman, Richard Olshen and Charles Stone he co-developed Classification and Regression Trees, published in 1984, and in 1996 he introduced Bagging, a method of averaging predictions across bootstrap samples to reduce variance. In 2001 he introduced Random Forests, an ensemble of randomized decision trees that became one of the most widely used machine learning algorithms, and published Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures, an influential essay on competing approaches to statistical inference. He died at his home in Berkeley, California, on July 5, 2005, following a prolonged illness.
people.name: Leo Breiman
people.moniker: Professor of Statistics, University of California, Berkeley

people.hook: Lisa Su has led AMD since October 2014, combining an electrical-engineering research background with semiconductor operations experience to turn the company from a distant also-ran into a primary supplier of AI accelerator hardware. Her MI300 and MI400 series GPUs gave large AI labs and cloud providers a credible second source of high-end accelerators alongside Nvidia. Su holds three degrees in electrical engineering from MIT and built her career through technical and general-management roles at Texas Instruments, IBM, and Freescale Semiconductor before joining AMD in 2012. She was named Time's CEO of the Year in 2024 and continues to set AMD's AI infrastructure roadmap, from CES keynotes to plans for trillion-parameter-scale training clusters.
people.name: Lisa Su
people.moniker: Chair and Chief Executive Officer, AMD

people.hook: Llion Jones grew up in Wales and earned a master's degree in advanced computer science from the University of Birmingham. He joined Google in 2012, first working as a software engineer on YouTube before moving into machine intelligence and natural language research around 2015. In 2017 he was one of eight Google researchers who co-authored Attention Is All You Need, the paper that introduced the Transformer architecture now underlying most large language models. He spent nearly twelve years at Google, then left in August 2023, citing frustration with internal bureaucracy and difficulty getting access to compute and data. He co-founded Sakana AI in Tokyo that year with fellow ex-Google researcher David Ha, taking the role of Chief Technology Officer and pursuing nature-inspired approaches to AI research as an alternative to simply building ever larger models.
people.name: Llion Jones
people.moniker: Co-founder and CTO, Sakana AI

people.hook: Lotfi Zadeh was born in Baku and later studied in Tehran before completing further degrees at MIT and Columbia University. He spent nine years on the electrical engineering faculty at Columbia before moving to the University of California, Berkeley in 1959, where he later chaired the Electrical Engineering Department from 1963 to 1968 and helped rename it the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences. In 1965 he published the paper Fuzzy Sets in the journal Information and Control, introducing a mathematical framework for representing categories that admit degrees of membership rather than strict true or false boundaries. That single paper launched fuzzy set theory and, later, fuzzy logic, which spread from control engineering into consumer electronics, decision analysis and approaches to reasoning under uncertainty in artificial intelligence. Zadeh remained a prolific researcher at Berkeley for the rest of his career, publishing more than two hundred papers and receiving numerous honors including the IEEE Medal of Honor and the Benjamin Franklin Medal.
people.name: Lotfi Zadeh
people.moniker: Founder of fuzzy set theory and fuzzy logic

people.hook: Lukasz Kaiser earned a master's degree from the University of Wroclaw in Poland and a PhD from RWTH Aachen University in Germany in 2008, working on logic and automata theory. He then spent time as a tenured researcher at Paris Diderot University before joining Google Brain in 2013. There he helped build the TensorFlow system and later co-created the Tensor2Tensor and Trax libraries used for sequence modeling research. In 2017 he co-authored Attention Is All You Need, contributing to the Transformer architecture that reshaped natural language processing. He later moved to OpenAI, where he worked as a research scientist and was credited as the long context lead on the GPT-4 project, helping extend how much text the model could take into account at once.
people.name: Lukasz Kaiser
people.moniker: Research scientist, OpenAI, and co-author of the Transformer

people.hook: Beck has spent over 17 years inside Daimler's IT organisation, running IT for Daimler Trucks Asia and Mitsubishi Fuso from Tokyo before becoming CIO of Daimler Truck North America in 2018, where he also now heads IT for autonomous driving. He speaks German, English, French, and Spanish.
people.name: Lutz Beck
people.moniker: CIO, Daimler Truck North America

people.hook: Margaret Mitchell is an AI researcher whose work focuses on documentation and transparency practices meant to make machine learning systems more accountable. Working across natural language processing and computer vision, she has held research roles at Microsoft Research, Google, and now Hugging Face. In 2018 she was the lead author of Model Cards for Model Reporting, a paper written with a team of Google and academic researchers, including Timnit Gebru, that proposed short standardized documents to accompany released machine learning models describing how they perform across different conditions and demographic groups. The model card format she helped design was later adopted widely across the AI industry. At Hugging Face she works on the company's Society and Ethics research efforts and contributes to open research initiatives such as the BigScience and BigCode workshops. Her research continues to center on practical tools, such as model documentation and bias evaluation methods, that let developers and the public better understand what a given AI system does and does not do well.
people.name: Margaret Mitchell
people.moniker: AI ethics researcher and co-creator of Model Cards

people.hook: Mark Chen has been at OpenAI since 2018, moving from quantitative trading into leading some of the company's most visible research programs. He co-led the team that built DALL-E, directed the vision work that gave GPT-4 its multimodal capabilities, and oversaw Codex, the model behind GitHub Copilot. In March 2025 OpenAI named him Chief Research Officer, a role focused on integrating research and product development so new capabilities move into deployment faster. He also coaches the USA Computing Olympiad team, a pastime that tracks with his own path through competitive mathematics and computer science at MIT.
people.name: Mark Chen
people.moniker: Chief Research Officer, OpenAI

people.hook: Marvin Minsky earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics from Harvard in 1950 and a PhD in mathematics from Princeton in 1954, having already built SNARC, an early neural network learning machine, as a student in 1951. In 1955 he joined John McCarthy, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon in writing the proposal for the 1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence, and in 1959 he co-founded what became the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory with McCarthy, directing it for many years. In 1969, with Seymour Papert, Minsky published Perceptrons, a rigorous mathematical analysis of the capabilities and limits of a simple class of neural networks that influenced the direction of AI research for years afterward. He later developed frame theory as a way of representing knowledge in AI systems, and in 1985 published Society of Mind, arguing that intelligence emerges from the interaction of many simple, specialized processes rather than any single mechanism. Minsky received the ACM A.M. Turing Award in 1969 for his central role in creating, shaping and advancing the field of artificial intelligence.
people.name: Marvin Minsky
people.moniker: Co-founded the MIT AI Lab and shaped decades of artificial intelligence research

people.hook: Wallace serves as President and CEO of Huston-Tillotson University in Austin, Texas, a historically Black university.
people.name: Melva Wallace
people.moniker: President and CEO, Huston-Tillotson University

people.hook: Michael I. Jordan earned a master's degree in mathematics from Arizona State University and a PhD in cognitive science from the University of California, San Diego in 1985. He joined the faculty of MIT in 1988, before moving to the University of California, Berkeley in 1998. At Berkeley he holds the Pehong Chen Distinguished Professorship jointly in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences and the Department of Statistics. His research connects statistics, optimization and computer science, with major contributions to probabilistic graphical models, variational inference and Bayesian nonparametric methods that shaped how modern machine learning systems reason under uncertainty. He has also been an outspoken voice pushing back on hype around artificial general intelligence, arguing in his widely read 2018 essay that the field needs a genuine engineering discipline built around real world human centered systems rather than science fiction narratives about human imitative AI.
