people.name: Michael I. Jordan
people.moniker: Pehong Chen Distinguished Professor, UC Berkeley

people.hook: Tripathi has spent his career on the unglamorous but consequential work of making health data actually move between systems, first from the policy side as the U.S. government's top health IT official, and now from inside a leading hospital system, applying that same interoperability and governance discipline to how AI gets deployed in clinical care.
people.name: Micky Tripathi
people.moniker: Federal Architect of Health AI Policy

people.hook: Mustafa Suleyman was born in London in 1984 and studied at the University of Oxford. In 2010 he co-founded DeepMind, an artificial intelligence research lab that Google acquired in 2014, where he went on to lead applied AI and policy work. After leaving Google in 2019 and a period as a venture partner at Greylock, he co-founded Inflection AI in March 2022 with Reid Hoffman and Karen Simonyan, building the Pi personal assistant and the Inflection-2.5 model. In 2023 he published The Coming Wave, a book arguing that AI and synthetic biology pose a containment problem for governments and societies. In March 2024 he joined Microsoft as CEO of Microsoft AI, leading the Copilot consumer AI effort, and he has continued to write and speak about what he calls building humanist superintelligence.
people.name: Mustafa Suleyman
people.moniker: CEO, Microsoft AI

people.hook: Nick Bostrom is a Swedish philosopher who has shaped how both academics and the public think about the long term risks and possibilities of advanced technology. He trained across physics, computational neuroscience, and philosophy at the universities of Gothenburg, Stockholm, and King's College London, and completed a PhD in philosophy at the London School of Economics in 2000. In 2002 he published the paper Existential Risks, which introduced a systematic taxonomy of the ways humanity's long term potential could be destroyed or permanently curtailed. In 2005 he founded and directed the Future of Humanity Institute at Oxford University, building it from three researchers into a center that helped incubate the fields of AI safety and effective altruism before it closed in 2024. His 2014 book Superintelligence, Paths, Dangers, Strategies became a New York Times bestseller and is widely credited with moving concerns about advanced AI from niche discussion into mainstream academic and public debate. He continues this work as founder of the Macrostrategy Research Initiative, and published the book Deep Utopia in 2024.
people.name: Nick Bostrom
people.moniker: Philosopher of existential risk and superintelligence

people.hook: Niki Parmar earned a bachelor's degree in information technology from the Pune Institute of Computer Technology in India, then a master's degree in computer science from the University of Southern California. She joined Google in 2015 as an engineer and research scientist, working on end to end deep learning systems for natural language processing. In 2017, reportedly the youngest member of her team and the only one without a PhD, she co-authored Attention Is All You Need, the paper that introduced the Transformer architecture. She spent close to seven years at Google before co-founding Adept AI Labs in 2022 as Chief Technology Officer, building enterprise workflow automation tools, and then co-founding Essential AI in 2023 to build full stack AI products for automating data processing, with backing from Google and Nvidia. She has since also worked as a member of technical staff at Anthropic on reliable and interpretable AI systems.
people.name: Niki Parmar
people.moniker: Co-founder, Essential AI

people.hook: Nils Nilsson earned his PhD in electrical engineering from Stanford in 1958, then served in the United States Air Force before joining SRI International, where he spent 23 years building foundational tools for artificial intelligence. At SRI he co-invented the A* search algorithm and the STRIPS automated planning system, and co-directed Shakey, one of the first mobile robots able to perceive its surroundings, plan, and act. He returned to Stanford in 1985 and chaired its Computer Science Department until 1990, later becoming the Kumagai Professor of Engineering, Emeritus. Nilsson wrote nine books on artificial intelligence, including the 2010 history The Quest for Artificial Intelligence, and served as president of AAAI. He died in 2019 in Medford, Oregon, at age 86.
people.name: Nils Nilsson
people.moniker: AI pioneer, Stanford University and SRI International

people.hook: Noam Shazeer joined Google in 2000, where he first worked on improving the search engine's spelling correction and helped develop the PHIL algorithm that became central to Google AdSense. Over the next two decades he moved into deep learning, co-authoring a paper on sparsely gated mixture of experts models in 2016 and then, in 2017, co-authoring Attention Is All You Need, where he designed the multi-head attention mechanism at the core of the Transformer. He went on to create Mesh-TensorFlow in 2018 for training large Transformers across many machines, co-authored the T5 model in 2019, and contributed to Google's LaMDA dialogue system. In 2021 he left Google to co-found Character.AI with Daniel De Freitas, serving as its CEO and building one of the first consumer chatbots built on Transformer technology. In August 2024 he returned to Google as part of a licensing deal with Character.AI, rejoining Google DeepMind's research team, and later co-led development of the Gemini model as Vice President of Engineering before departing for OpenAI in June 2026.
people.name: Noam Shazeer
people.moniker: AI researcher, OpenAI

people.hook: Arbaugh went from a diving accident that left him paralyzed to becoming, at 29, the first person on Earth to use a brain implant to control a computer in daily life, turning his own recovery into the most closely watched real-world test of whether brain-computer interfaces can restore independence.
people.name: Noland Arbaugh
people.moniker: The World's First Neuralink Patient

people.hook: Norbert Wiener was a mathematical prodigy who earned a bachelor's degree from Tufts College at 14 and a PhD in philosophy from Harvard at 19, then studied with Bertrand Russell in Cambridge and David Hilbert in Gottingen. He joined MIT's Department of Mathematics in 1919 and remained there for 45 years, doing foundational work in stochastic processes, harmonic analysis, and what became known as the Wiener process. During the Second World War he worked on statistical prediction methods for anti-aircraft fire control, research that pushed him toward a broader theory of control and communication. In 1948 he published Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine, founding the field of cybernetics and giving later computing and AI research a vocabulary for feedback loops. His 1950 book The Human Use of Human Beings extended these ideas to society, warning early about the social effects of automation. He became an MIT Institute Professor in 1959 and died in 1964 while traveling in Stockholm, Sweden.
people.name: Norbert Wiener
people.moniker: Founder of cybernetics, MIT

people.hook: Gelsinger's career traces the arc of modern computing hardware itself: chief architect of a landmark Intel processor in his twenties, the company's first CTO, then, decades later, recalled as CEO to fight for American chip manufacturing leadership just as AI's compute demands made semiconductors a national priority.
people.name: Pat Gelsinger
people.moniker: Engineer Who Led Intel's Turnaround Attempt

people.hook: Paul Christiano holds a PhD in statistical learning theory from UC Berkeley. While working on the alignment team at OpenAI, he was a co-author and principal architect of the 2017 paper Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences, which introduced the technique now known as reinforcement learning from human feedback, using human comparisons between possible outputs to train reinforcement learning systems. That approach was later adapted to fine-tune large language models and became a standard part of how systems like ChatGPT are trained to follow instructions and match human judgment. In 2021 he left OpenAI to found the Alignment Research Center (ARC), a nonprofit that develops theoretical and empirical methods for understanding and evaluating advanced AI systems, including work on eliciting latent knowledge from neural networks. He was named to the Time 100 Most Influential People in AI in 2023, and in 2024 he began advising the U.S. government's AI safety evaluation work through what is now NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation.
people.name: Paul Christiano
people.moniker: Founder, Alignment Research Center

people.hook: Paul Werbos studied economics at the London School of Economics before earning a PhD from Harvard University in 1974, where his dissertation, Beyond Regression, described how the chain rule for ordered derivatives could train neural network-like models, work later recognized as the first description of backpropagation. Through the 1980s he worked as an econometric forecasting analyst at the U.S. Energy Information Administration, applying related statistical modeling techniques. In 1988 he joined the National Science Foundation as a program director, where he spent over two decades directing funding for research on adaptive systems and neural networks before retiring in 2015. His dissertation was later republished as the book The Roots of Backpropagation (Wiley, 1994), and he went on to develop related ideas under the name adaptive dynamic programming, connecting neural networks with dynamic programming based control. In 2011 the International Neural Network Society gave him its Hebb Award, its highest honor.
people.name: Paul Werbos
people.moniker: Originator of backpropagation for neural networks

people.hook: Percy Liang is a computer scientist whose work has shaped how the field measures and understands large language models. He earned a Bachelor of Science from MIT in 2004 and a PhD in computer science from the University of California, Berkeley in 2011, advised by Michael Jordan and Dan Klein. He joined the faculty of Stanford University, where he is a professor of computer science with a courtesy appointment in statistics, and became director of the Stanford Center for Research on Foundation Models. In 2022 he led a large multi institution team in creating Holistic Evaluation of Language Models, a benchmarking framework designed to standardize how language models are assessed across accuracy, robustness, fairness and other dimensions at once. He has also built infrastructure for reproducible AI research, including CodaLab Worksheets, and teaches a widely followed Stanford course on building language models from scratch.
people.name: Percy Liang
people.moniker: Director, Stanford Center for Research on Foundation Models

people.hook: Mehrotra built Allstate's entire AI Center of Excellence from the ground up, an 80-plus person team and a multi-year generative AI strategy, and now applies that same enterprise-AI playbook as Chief AI Officer at U.S. Bank.
people.name: Prashant Mehrotra
people.moniker: Chief AI Officer at U.S. Bank

people.hook: Naga's entire executive career was built inside two companies that run some of the largest real-time systems on Earth, LinkedIn and Uber, rising internally at Uber over eleven years to become CTO of a platform operating across cities, countries, and hundreds of millions of users.
people.name: Praveen Neppalli Naga
people.moniker: Chief Technology Officer at Uber

people.hook: Raj Reddy earned a bachelor's degree in engineering from Guindy Engineering College at the University of Madras in 1958, a master's from the University of New South Wales in 1960, and a PhD in computer science from Stanford University in 1966. He joined Carnegie Mellon University as an associate professor in 1969 and led development of the Hearsay speech understanding systems, early efforts to combine multiple knowledge sources for recognizing connected speech. In 1979 he became the founding director of Carnegie Mellon's Robotics Institute, building it into one of the world's leading robotics research centers, and later served as dean of the School of Computer Science from 1991 to 1999. In 1994 he shared the ACM Turing Award with Edward Feigenbaum for pioneering the design of large-scale artificial intelligence systems. He has also worked on extending computing access to underserved populations, including projects aimed at low-cost computing and digital libraries for developing regions.
people.name: Raj Reddy
people.moniker: Turing Award laureate, speech recognition and robotics pioneer

people.hook: Raquel Urtasun is a computer scientist and entrepreneur who has spent her career at the intersection of computer vision, robotics, and self driving technology. She earned her PhD in computer science from the Ecole Polytechnique Federale de Lausanne in 2006, then completed postdoctoral research at MIT and UC Berkeley before joining the Toyota Technological Institute at Chicago as an assistant professor. She later became a Canada Research Chair in Machine Learning and Computer Vision at the University of Toronto, where she remains a full professor and is a co-founder of the Vector Institute for AI. From 2017 to 2021 she served as Chief Scientist and Head of Research and Development at Uber's Advanced Technologies Group in Toronto, leading self driving vehicle research. After leaving Uber, she founded Waabi, a company building AI first software for autonomous trucks and robotaxis, where she serves as Founder and CEO.
people.name: Raquel Urtasun
people.moniker: Founder and CEO, Waabi

people.hook: Ummadisetti has been building production generative AI systems, RAG pipelines, model fine-tuning, agentic platforms, since before the term agentic AI entered general use. At Toyota North America he leads the function responsible for autonomous AI agents in one of the world's largest automotive manufacturers, while his seat on the LangChain advisory board gives him direct influence on the open-source tooling that most agentic systems are built on.
people.name: Ravi Chandu Ummadisetti
people.moniker: Head of Agentic AI at Toyota North America

people.hook: Ray Kurzweil is an American inventor, computer scientist, and author known both for his technical contributions to pattern recognition technology and for his predictions about the future of artificial intelligence. Born in Queens, New York in 1948 and trained in computer science and literature at MIT, he began founding technology companies in 1973 and in 1976 introduced the Kurzweil Reading Machine, the first device able to convert printed text into spoken words for blind and visually impaired users. He went on to develop optical character recognition software able to read text in any typeface, along with early text to speech and speech recognition systems, work recognized with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation in 1999 and induction into the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 2002. Alongside his inventing career, Kurzweil became a widely read futurist, publishing books including The Age of Spiritual Machines and The Singularity Is Near that argue technological change is accelerating toward a point where machine intelligence will exceed human intelligence. In 2012 he joined Google, where he now holds the title of principal researcher and AI visionary, leading a team working on natural language understanding.
people.name: Ray Kurzweil
people.moniker: Inventor, futurist, and Google AI researcher

people.hook: Solomon's path from electrical engineering to venture investment to AI partnerships at Airbus traces the evolution of applied AI from semiconductor and IoT adjacencies into aerospace's core technology strategy. At Airbus she shapes the partnerships and technology decisions that will determine how autonomous systems, AI-assisted design, and intelligent maintenance enter one of the most safety-critical industries in the world.
people.name: Reena Solomon
people.moniker: Head of AI Partnerships at Airbus, North America

people.hook: Richard Sutton studied psychology at Stanford before moving into computer science at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, where he earned his PhD in 1984 working with Andrew Barto on the mathematical foundations of reinforcement learning. He went on to research positions in industry and academia before joining the University of Alberta, where he now holds the AITF Chair in Reinforcement Learning and Artificial Intelligence and serves as Chief Scientific Advisor to the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute. With Barto he wrote Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, the field's standard textbook, first published in 1998 and revised in 2018. He also holds a part-time research role at Google DeepMind and in 2022 helped found Keen Technologies with John Carmack to pursue artificial general intelligence. His 2019 essay The Bitter Lesson argued that general, computation-driven learning methods outperform approaches built on human-designed domain knowledge, a claim that shaped much of the field's later direction. In 2024 he and Barto received the ACM A.M. Turing Award for developing the conceptual and algorithmic foundations of reinforcement learning.
people.name: Richard Sutton
people.moniker: Professor of Computing Science, University of Alberta

people.hook: Schwartz runs the innovation function at one of the country's leading academic hospital systems, where her job is turning AI tools, from ambient clinical documentation to decision support, from vendor pitches into things doctors and nurses actually trust and use at the bedside.
people.name: Roberta Schwartz
people.moniker: Hospital Innovation Chief Bringing AI to the Bedside

people.hook: Robin Rombach is the lead author of the Latent Diffusion Models paper produced with the CompVis group at LMU Munich, the research that became the technical basis for Stable Diffusion. After a physics degree at Heidelberg and a PhD at LMU Munich, he continued the work as Research Director at Stability AI before leaving in 2024. In August 2024 he co-founded Black Forest Labs with two of his Latent Diffusion co-authors, Patrick Esser and Andreas Blattmann, releasing the FLUX.1 image model on launch day. He now runs Black Forest Labs as CEO from labs in Freiburg and San Francisco, and in 2026 spoke at the G7 alongside heads of state to argue for keeping frontier visual AI development open.
people.name: Robin Rombach
people.moniker: Co-founder and CEO, Black Forest Labs

people.hook: Rodney Brooks trained in pure mathematics at Flinders University in his native Australia before earning a PhD in computer science from Stanford in 1981. After research positions at Carnegie Mellon, MIT and Stanford, he joined the MIT faculty in 1984 and later directed the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory and then the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. His 1986 paper describing the subsumption architecture argued that intelligent robot behavior could emerge from layered, reactive control systems rather than centralized symbolic planning, a challenge to the AI orthodoxy of the time that helped found the field of behavior-based robotics. He put that thinking into commercial practice by co-founding iRobot in 1990 with Colin Angle and Helen Greiner, whose Roomba vacuum became one of the first robots to reach mass consumer markets. In 2008 he founded Heartland Robotics, later renamed Rethink Robotics, to build the Baxter and Sawyer collaborative robots for factory work, and in 2019 he founded Robust.AI to continue work on practical, everyday robotics.
people.name: Rodney Brooks
people.moniker: Roboticist and co-founder of iRobot and Rethink Robotics

people.hook: Whitworth arrived at privacy from communications law, FCC staff, telecom practice, online business counsel, before building a financial-sector privacy career that now spans one of the largest U.S. bank mergers. At Truist he oversees global privacy, technology compliance, and AI compliance across the full institution and its affiliates, making him an early practitioner of the combined privacy-AI governance function that regulators are now formalizing.
people.name: Ron Whitworth
people.moniker: Chief Privacy Officer at Truist

people.hook: Rumman Chowdhury is a data scientist who has built her career around auditing artificial intelligence systems for bias and holding the companies that deploy them accountable. She holds a PhD and led artificial intelligence ethics work at the consulting firm Accenture before joining Twitter, where she served as engineering director of the company's Machine Learning Ethics, Transparency and Accountability team and helped pioneer the use of algorithmic bias bounty programs, in which outside researchers are invited to find and report harms in a company's AI systems. She went on to found Humane Intelligence, a nonprofit that designs large scale, structured red teaming exercises to evaluate AI systems for fairness and safety in partnership with governments and industry. The Biden Administration appointed her the US Department of State's Science Envoy for Artificial Intelligence, a role in which she advises on AI governance issues internationally. Chowdhury stepped down as chief executive of Humane Intelligence in 2025 and remains an affiliate of Harvard's Berkman Klein Center for Internet and Society.
people.name: Rumman Chowdhury
people.moniker: AI ethics leader and pioneer of algorithmic red-teaming

people.hook: Katti built his career on the unglamorous but essential problem of moving data efficiently, first in academic networking research, then running Intel's networking hardware division, and now at OpenAI, where the physical compute infrastructure behind frontier AI models is his direct responsibility.
people.name: Sachin Katti
people.moniker: OpenAI's Head of Compute and Former Stanford Networking Professor

people.hook: Nandy spent over 15 years building the infrastructure behind Google's core advertising and analytics businesses, systems used by billions of people, before leading product and engineering at Okta's identity platform and now steering Docusign's shift toward AI-driven agreement management as CTO.
people.name: Sagnik Nandy
people.moniker: Chief Technology Officer at Docusign, Former Google VP

people.hook: Altman turned artificial intelligence from a research field into a consumer phenomenon and a geopolitical agenda item. ChatGPT's November 2022 launch under his leadership put generative AI in hundreds of millions of hands, and his Senate testimony six months later, a CEO asking to be regulated, set the tone for the global governance debate this library documents.
people.name: Sam Altman
people.moniker: The Face of the AI Boom

people.hook: Sanjay Ghemawat earned an SB from Cornell University in 1987 and a PhD in computer science from MIT in 1995, advised by Barbara Liskov and Frans Kaashoek. Before joining Google in late 1999 he worked as a member of the research staff at Digital Equipment Corporation's Systems Research Center in Palo Alto. At Google he became one of the principal architects of the distributed systems that made the company's scale possible, co-designing the Google File System in 2003, MapReduce with Jeff Dean in 2004, Bigtable in 2006, and Spanner, Google's globally distributed database, in 2012. He has also contributed to Protocol Buffers, LevelDB, TensorFlow, and the Pathways distributed machine learning system. He now holds the title of Senior Fellow at Google, among the company's most senior technical positions, and has spent more than two decades building the infrastructure layer underneath Google's products and, later, its large-scale AI training systems.
people.name: Sanjay Ghemawat
people.moniker: Senior Fellow, Google

people.hook: Thrun proved autonomous driving was possible by winning DARPA's toughest robotics prize, then built the Google program that turned that proof into Waymo, the industry's leading self-driving company, while separately co-founding Udacity to bring university-grade technical education online.
people.name: Sebastian Thrun
people.moniker: Founder of Google's Self-Driving Car Project and Udacity

people.hook: Sebastien Bubeck trained in France, earning his PhD in mathematics at the University of Lille and receiving the Jacques Neveu prize for the best French doctoral thesis in probability and statistics. He worked as an assistant professor in Princeton University's Department of Operations Research and Financial Engineering before joining Microsoft Research in Redmond, where he leads work in the Machine Learning Foundations group and holds the title of Vice President and Distinguished Scientist. His early research centered on convex optimization and multi-armed bandit problems, work recognized with an Alfred P. Sloan Research Fellowship in 2015 and multiple best paper awards. He co-authored the 2015 monograph Convex Optimization: Algorithms and Complexity. His research focus shifted toward large language models, and in March 2023 he led the Microsoft Research team that wrote Sparks of Artificial General Intelligence, an early evaluation of GPT-4 that argued the model showed markedly more general capability than earlier systems. He also helped develop Microsoft's Phi family of small, efficiently trained language models.
people.name: Sebastien Bubeck
people.moniker: Vice President and Distinguished Scientist, Microsoft Research

people.hook: Sepp Hochreiter's 1991 diploma thesis at the Technical University of Munich diagnosed why deep and recurrent neural networks of the time failed to learn long-range dependencies, an analysis now known as the vanishing gradient problem. Working with his advisor Jurgen Schmidhuber, he developed Long Short-Term Memory networks as a solution, publishing the architecture in Neural Computation in 1997. LSTM became the dominant approach to sequence modeling for two decades, powering speech recognition and machine translation systems before the rise of Transformer models. After research positions at the University of Colorado Boulder and the Technical University of Berlin, Hochreiter joined Johannes Kepler University Linz, where he directed the Institute of Bioinformatics from 2006 and has led the Institute for Machine Learning since 2018. He also works on applying machine learning to genomics and other bioinformatics problems. In 2021 he received the IEEE Computational Intelligence Society Neural Networks Pioneer Award. He later founded NXAI, a Linz-based company building xLSTM, an extended memory architecture positioned as an alternative to Transformer models for sequence and time-series tasks.
people.name: Sepp Hochreiter
people.moniker: Head, Institute for Machine Learning, Johannes Kepler University Linz

people.hook: Sergey Levine studied computer science at Stanford University, earning his BS and MS in 2009 and completing a PhD there in 2014. He joined the Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences faculty at UC Berkeley in 2016, where he directs the Robotic Artificial Intelligence and Learning (RAIL) lab. His research develops algorithms that let autonomous agents, especially physical robots, learn complex behaviors directly from experience using deep reinforcement learning rather than hand-engineered controllers, work that has shaped how the field approaches robotic manipulation, locomotion and autonomous vehicle control. In 2024 he joined the robotics startup Physical Intelligence, contributing to the team behind pi-zero, a general-purpose foundation model intended to control many different kinds of robots across a range of tasks.
people.name: Sergey Levine
people.moniker: Professor of robotics and reinforcement learning, UC Berkeley

people.hook: Seymour Papert earned a PhD in mathematics from the University of Witwatersrand in South Africa in 1952 and a second PhD from Cambridge University in 1958, then studied children's cognitive development with Jean Piaget at the University of Geneva. He joined MIT in 1963, became a professor of applied mathematics in 1967, and co-directed MIT's Artificial Intelligence Laboratory with Marvin Minsky, with whom he co-authored the 1969 book Perceptrons, an influential mathematical analysis of early neural networks. Drawing on his work with Piaget, Papert co-developed the Logo programming language and its turtle graphics for children, and in his 1980 book Mindstorms: Children, Computers, and Powerful Ideas he set out constructionism, an educational theory holding that children learn best by building and creating things themselves. He became a founding faculty member of the MIT Media Lab in 1985 and in 2004 co-founded the One Laptop per Child initiative to extend computing access to children in developing countries. After suffering a serious brain injury in a 2006 accident in Hanoi, Vietnam, he died in 2016 at his home in Maine.
people.name: Seymour Papert
people.moniker: Educational technology pioneer, MIT Media Lab

people.hook: Shane Legg studied computer science at the University of Waikato and completed a master's degree at the University of Auckland before pursuing doctoral research at the Dalle Molle Institute for Artificial Intelligence Research (IDSIA) under Marcus Hutter. His PhD thesis, Machine Super Intelligence, set out an early formal research agenda for artificial general intelligence, and with Hutter he proposed a mathematical definition of machine intelligence that became a reference point for later work on measuring progress toward general AI. In 2010 he co-founded DeepMind Technologies with Demis Hassabis and Mustafa Suleyman, a company Google acquired in 2014. He has written publicly, including on his personal blog, about probabilistic forecasts for when machine intelligence might reach human levels. He was appointed Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 2019 for services to artificial intelligence. When DeepMind and Google's Brain team merged in April 2023 to form Google DeepMind, Legg remained part of the unit's core leadership group and continued his research role focused on artificial general intelligence.
people.name: Shane Legg
people.moniker: Chief AGI Scientist, Google DeepMind

people.hook: Soumith Chintala spent eleven years at Facebook and Meta building the infrastructure researchers actually use, and in 2016 that work became PyTorch, a framework Meta's own engineering blog credits him with co-creating. PyTorch went from a research tool to the default choice for training large language models and most of the vision and generative models that followed it. In January 2026 he left the company where he built his career to become Chief Technology Officer at Mira Murati's Thinking Machines Lab, taking on AI infrastructure and research at a new frontier lab. He also holds an affiliation at NYU, the university where he earned his master's degree under Yann LeCun, working there on home robotics with Lerrel Pinto.
people.name: Soumith Chintala
people.moniker: Chief Technology Officer, Thinking Machines Lab

people.hook: Venkatesan has spent 25 years running the technology behind some of the largest consumer platforms in commerce and advertising, eBay, StubHub, Marketo, Yahoo, Walmart, and now PayPal, where he leads AI and machine learning across the company's entire payments ecosystem.
people.name: Srini Venkatesan
people.moniker: EVP and Chief Technology Officer at PayPal

people.hook: Preston moved from running two federal agencies during the 2008 financial crisis to leading Goodwill Industries, where he has directed the organization's push to use AI-enabled training tools to help workers displaced by automation move into new careers, applying crisis-era public administration experience to AI's labor disruption.
people.name: Steve Preston
people.moniker: Cabinet Official Turned Nonprofit CEO

people.hook: Kirkeberg spent over a decade building the cloud infrastructure underneath Norway's sovereign wealth fund before pivoting to build its AI function from nothing, growing it into a 71-member AI Ambassador network across Oslo, London, New York, and Singapore with measured efficiency gains rather than speculative claims.
people.name: Stian Kirkeberg
people.moniker: Head of AI & ML at Norway's Sovereign Wealth Fund

people.hook: Stuart Russell is Distinguished Professor of Computer Science at UC Berkeley, where he also holds the Smith-Zadeh Professorship in Engineering and a professorship in Cognitive Science. With Peter Norvig he co-authored Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, first published in 1995 and now in multiple editions, which became the standard textbook used to teach AI in universities worldwide. In 2016 he founded the Center for Human-Compatible AI (CHAI) at Berkeley, a research lab devoted to redesigning AI systems around explicit uncertainty about human preferences rather than fixed objectives, on the argument that optimizing a fixed goal too well is what makes highly capable AI systems dangerous. He set out that argument for a general audience in his 2019 book Human Compatible: Artificial Intelligence and the Problem of Control, and in 2021 he delivered the BBC's Reith Lectures on living with artificial intelligence. He holds an OBE and is a Fellow of the Royal Society, and also serves as Professor of Computational Precision Health at UCSF and an Honorary Fellow of Wadham College, Oxford.
people.name: Stuart Russell
people.moniker: Distinguished Professor of Computer Science, UC Berkeley

people.hook: Takeo Kanade earned his PhD in electrical engineering from Kyoto University in 1974 and taught there before joining Carnegie Mellon University in 1980. He directed Carnegie Mellon's Robotics Institute from 1992 to 2001 and now holds the title of U.A. and Helen Whitaker University Professor of Robotics and Computer Science there. Across a research career spanning computer vision and robotics, he pioneered early facial recognition methods, multi-baseline stereo vision, the factorization method for recovering 3D shape and motion from images, and virtualized reality techniques for capturing 3D scenes from multiple cameras. He also led Carnegie Mellon's Navlab autonomous vehicle program, including a 1995 cross-country demonstration drive in which the vehicle steered itself for most of the route from Pittsburgh to San Diego. In 2016 he received the Kyoto Prize in Advanced Technology for his contributions to the field.
people.name: Takeo Kanade
people.moniker: Computer vision and robotics pioneer, Carnegie Mellon University

people.hook: Terence Tao is a mathematician whose work spans harmonic analysis, partial differential equations, number theory and combinatorics, and who has more recently turned his attention to using computers and formal proof systems to assist mathematical research. He completed his PhD at Princeton University in 1996 under Elias Stein and joined UCLA the same year, where he has been a full professor since 2000 and has held the James and Carol Collins Chair in Mathematics since 2007. In 2006 he received the Fields Medal, mathematics' highest honor, for contributions across several areas of analysis and combinatorics. In November 2023, after co-authoring a proof of the Polynomial Freiman-Ruzsa conjecture over finite fields with Tim Gowers, Ben Green and Freddie Manners, Tao led a rapid collaborative effort with Yael Dillies and Bhavik Mehta to formalize the entire proof in the Lean 4 proof assistant using a tool called Blueprint, completing the verification within weeks. He has continued to build public infrastructure for formalized mathematics, including a Lean companion to his own real analysis textbook and, in 2026, a registry called Palomar for tracking Lean verified proofs amid a rise in AI generated mathematical claims.
people.name: Terence Tao
people.moniker: Professor of Mathematics, UCLA

people.hook: Terry Sejnowski earned a BS in physics from Case Western Reserve University and a PhD in physics from Princeton University, followed by postdoctoral work in biology at Princeton and in neurobiology at Harvard Medical School. In 1985 he co-authored A Learning Algorithm for Boltzmann Machines with David Ackley and Geoffrey Hinton, introducing a stochastic learning method for neural networks. Working with Charles Rosenberg, he then built NETtalk, a neural network that learned to convert written English text into speech sounds, published in 1987 in Complex Systems and widely cited as an early demonstration that distributed neural networks could learn a complex cognitive task from examples. In 1988 he moved to the Salk Institute for Biological Studies, where he now holds the Francis Crick Chair and directs the Computational Neurobiology Laboratory, with a joint appointment at the University of California, San Diego. He founded the journal Neural Computation in 1989 and has served as its editor-in-chief since, and in 2018 he co-authored the book The Deep Learning Revolution. He was elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 2010 and has since received the Gruber Neuroscience Prize and the Brain Prize.
people.name: Terry Sejnowski
people.moniker: Professor and Francis Crick Chair, Salk Institute for Biological Studies

people.hook: Thomas Wolf trained as a physicist, not a computer scientist, earning a PhD in statistical and quantum physics before spending five years as a patent attorney in Paris. He taught himself deep learning in 2015 and 2016 and used it to co-found Hugging Face, then helped build the Transformers library that became the standard interface to pretrained language models across the field. As the company's Chief Science Officer he has also driven its open-science side, including the BigScience workshop that produced the BLOOM model. In September 2026, Hugging Face agreed to be acquired by NVIDIA in a deal reported near thirteen billion dollars, a turn Wolf described on X as an outcome nobody at the company anticipated back in 2016.
people.name: Thomas Wolf
people.moniker: Co-founder and Chief Science Officer, Hugging Face

people.hook: Tianqi Chen built his reputation as a graduate student by creating tools that made machine learning systems faster and easier to deploy at scale. He earned bachelor's and master's degrees from Shanghai Jiao Tong University before completing a PhD at the University of Washington's Paul G. Allen School in 2019, advised by Carlos Guestrin. During his PhD he created XGBoost, a gradient boosting library that became a default choice for structured data problems in industry and machine learning competitions, and he co-created Apache MXNet, an early deep learning framework, and Apache TVM, a compiler that lets deep learning models run efficiently across many kinds of hardware. In 2019 he co-founded OctoML, later renamed OctoAI, serving as its chief technologist to commercialize the machine learning compilation techniques behind TVM, and the company was acquired by NVIDIA in 2024. He is now an Associate Professor in the Machine Learning and Computer Science Departments at Carnegie Mellon University and a Distinguished Engineer at NVIDIA, and he continues to lead open source projects including MLC-LLM for deploying large language models on everyday devices.
people.name: Tianqi Chen
people.moniker: Associate Professor, Carnegie Mellon University, and Distinguished Engineer, NVIDIA

people.hook: Tim Dettmers built his career on the wager that making large models run on far less hardware would open up who gets to do AI research at all. His PhD work at the University of Washington, advised by Luke Zettlemoyer, produced LLM.int8() in 2022 and then QLoRA in 2023, a method that let a 65 billion parameter language model be fine-tuned on a single 48 gigabyte GPU. He maintains bitsandbytes, the open-source quantization library those methods run on, and in 2024 he became an Assistant Professor at Carnegie Mellon University while continuing as a Research Scientist at the Allen Institute for AI. His own faculty page describes his focus as making foundation models accessible to researchers and practitioners by reducing their resource requirements.
people.name: Tim Dettmers
people.moniker: Assistant Professor, Carnegie Mellon University

people.hook: Latimer trained as a drilling and completion engineer at BHP Billiton before pairing an energy-track master's degree with an MBA at Stanford, then founded Fervo Energy, the enhanced-geothermal company applying oil-and-gas drilling techniques to clean baseload power. He has led the company for nearly nine years and was named a Presidential Leadership Scholar in 2022.
people.name: Tim Latimer
people.moniker: CEO, Fervo Energy

people.hook: O'Reilly has spent four decades doing the same thing under different names: spotting a technology shift before the industry has language for it, then naming it. 'Open source' and 'Web 2.0' both trace to conferences he convened, and his publishing house has been the technical-literacy backbone for the programmers who built the modern internet, and now AI.
people.name: Tim O'Reilly
people.moniker: Publisher Who Named Web 2.0 and the Open Source Movement

people.hook: Timnit Gebru is a computer scientist who has become one of the most prominent voices in AI ethics and accountability. She earned her PhD in computer vision from Stanford University, advised by Fei-Fei Li, after early work in circuit design and audio engineering at Apple. She then completed a postdoctoral fellowship in Microsoft Research's Fairness, Accountability, Transparency and Ethics group before joining Google in 2018, where she co-led the Ethical AI research team with Margaret Mitchell. Gebru left Google in December 2020 after a dispute over a research paper examining the risks of large language models, a departure that drew wide attention to tensions between AI ethics researchers and corporate priorities. In December 2021 she founded the Distributed AI Research Institute, an independent, interdisciplinary institute with researchers based across North America, Europe and Africa that studies the harms of current AI systems and researches alternative approaches. She also co-founded Black in AI, a nonprofit supporting Black researchers and students in artificial intelligence.
people.name: Timnit Gebru
people.moniker: Founder and Executive Director, DAIR

people.hook: Timothée Lacroix worked on Meta's LLaMA language models as a researcher at Facebook AI Research before leaving in 2023 to co-found Mistral AI with Arthur Mensch and Guillaume Lample. As Chief Technology Officer he leads the Paris-based company's research and technical direction, the work behind models like Mistral Large and the Le Chat assistant. Mistral positioned itself from the outset as a European counterweight to closed, US-based AI labs, releasing open-weight models such as Mistral 7B alongside its commercial offerings. Lacroix trained as a computer scientist at the Ecole Normale Superieure and holds a doctorate tied to the University of Paris-Est.
people.name: Timothée Lacroix
people.moniker: Co-founder and Chief Technology Officer, Mistral AI

people.hook: Gruber built a career in academic knowledge-representation research before co-founding Siri, whose acquisition by Apple in 2010 put conversational AI into hundreds of millions of pockets years before ChatGPT made the category mainstream, and he has argued ever since for AI designed to amplify human intelligence rather than substitute for it.
people.name: Tom Gruber
people.moniker: Co-Creator of Siri

people.hook: Tom Mitchell helped establish machine learning as an academic discipline in its own right. He earned a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from MIT in 1973 and a PhD from Stanford University in 1979, studying under Bruce Buchanan. After teaching at Rutgers University, he joined Carnegie Mellon University in 1986, where he became the E. Fredkin Professor and later the founding chair of the world's first Machine Learning Department in 2006. In 1997 he published the textbook Machine Learning, one of the first comprehensive textbooks in the field and still used in university courses. His later research pushed machine learning into new territory, including the Never-Ending Language Learner project, which continuously extracts facts from web text, and work using brain imaging to study how the brain represents word meaning. He has also studied the effects of AI on the labor market, co-chairing a National Academies report on AI and the future of work.
people.name: Tom Mitchell
fields: AI and the future of work
people.moniker: University Professor, Carnegie Mellon University Machine Learning Department

people.hook: Ambrozie has led digital transformation at three of the largest consumer-facing organizations in America, Ford, Disney Parks, and now CVS Health, bringing consumer-experience engineering discipline to bear on making AI-driven healthcare personalization work at national scale.
people.name: Tony Ambrozie
people.moniker: Healthcare's Digital and AI Transformation Executive

people.hook: Tri Dao's PhD work at Stanford, co-advised by Christopher Re and Stefano Ermon, produced FlashAttention, a fast, memory-efficient attention algorithm that cut a Transformer's memory use from quadratic to linear in sequence length. Presented at NeurIPS in 2022 and later extended in FlashAttention-2 and FlashAttention-3, it became a piece of infrastructure that most large language models now train and run on. He joined Together AI as a co-founder and Chief Scientist around the time he finished his PhD, and is also an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Princeton University, where he leads the Dao AI Lab.
people.name: Tri Dao
people.moniker: Assistant Professor, Princeton University, and Chief Scientist, Together AI

people.hook: Childers moved from Fortune 20 operations, Amazon's peak IT infrastructure and GE's global virtualization program, into the CIO seat at a precision aerospace manufacturer. His IoT initiative at Meyer Tool, measuring machine productivity and availability on the factory floor, is the kind of applied industrial AI that rarely makes headlines but represents the actual frontier of operational technology in advanced manufacturing.
people.name: Vern Childers
people.moniker: CIO at Meyer Tool

people.hook: Badrinarayanan helped write one of computer vision's most-cited deep learning papers, SegNet, before moving into frontier AI research at DeepMind, and now leads AI development at Wayve, applying end-to-end learned driving models rather than the hand-coded rule systems most autonomous vehicle companies rely on.
people.name: Vijay Badrinarayanan
people.moniker: Computer Vision Researcher Behind SegNet and Wayve's Self-Driving AI

people.hook: Vladimir Vapnik developed much of the mathematical foundation that modern machine learning still relies on. Born in Tashkent in the Soviet Union, he earned his doctorate in statistics from the Institute of Control Sciences in Moscow in 1964, where he later headed the computer science research department. Working with Alexey Chervonenkis, he developed what became known as Vapnik-Chervonenkis theory, a mathematical framework for understanding when and why a learning algorithm can generalize from training data to new examples. After moving to the United States, he joined AT&T Bell Labs, where he and colleagues including Corinna Cortes, Bernard Boser, and Isabelle Guyon turned his theoretical work into the support vector machine, a classification method described in a landmark 1995 paper with Cortes and in a US patent he shares with Boser and Guyon. He went on to hold research and teaching positions at NEC Laboratories, Royal Holloway University of London, Columbia University, and Facebook AI Research, continuing to develop and extend statistical learning theory.
people.name: Vladimir Vapnik
people.moniker: Co-inventor of the support vector machine and statistical learning theory

people.hook: Ellsworth graduated early from Stanford with a B.S. in Computer Science with Distinction, worked as a research engineer at Google DeepMind, and now leads initiatives related to search and agents as a Member of Technical Staff at OpenAI. He was a U.S. Presidential Scholar and a USA Biology Olympiad national finalist.
people.name: Will Ellsworth
people.moniker: Researcher, OpenAI

people.hook: Yangqing Jia was still a PhD student at UC Berkeley when he built Caffe, one of the first deep learning frameworks to open source its full code and model zoo, and it became a standard tool for computer vision research for several years. He carried that pattern through a string of AI infrastructure roles, co-creating Google's Inception architecture at Google Brain, building Facebook's internal AI platform and co-creating Caffe2 and ONNX there, then running Alibaba Cloud's computing platform and its DAMO Academy systems lab. He founded Lepton AI in 2023, sold it to NVIDIA in 2025, left NVIDIA in mid-2026 over the company's decision not to open source the platform, and that July launched Intent Lab, an autonomous software engineering startup, with several former Lepton AI colleagues.
people.name: Yangqing Jia
people.moniker: Founder and CEO, Intent Lab

people.hook: Yann LeCun helped build the technique that underlies most of today's computer vision systems. He earned a PhD in computer science from Universite Pierre et Marie Curie in Paris in 1987, working on early ideas that fed into backpropagation based neural network training. At AT&T Bell Labs starting in 1988, he developed convolutional neural networks and built LeNet, a system for reading handwritten digits that was later deployed commercially to process a large share of checks handled by US banks. He went on to become a professor at New York University's Courant Institute, founding the NYU Center for Data Science, and in 2013 joined Facebook, later Meta, as founding director and then Chief AI Scientist of its AI research division. In 2018 he shared the ACM A.M. Turing Award with Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio for their work on deep learning. He left Meta in November 2025 after roughly twelve years to launch Advanced Machine Intelligence Labs, a venture focused on building AI systems around world models rather than only predicting text.
people.name: Yann LeCun
people.moniker: Executive Chair, Advanced Machine Intelligence Labs, and former Chief AI Scientist, Meta

people.hook: Yejin Choi is a computer scientist known for advancing commonsense reasoning and evaluation methods in natural language processing. She earned a bachelor's degree in computer engineering from Seoul National University and a PhD in computer science from Cornell University, then built her academic career at the University of Washington, where she held the Brett Helsel Career Development Professorship from 2020 to 2023 and the Wissner-Slivka Chair from 2023 to 2024. Her research has focused on giving machines the kind of everyday, common sense knowledge that humans take for granted, and on building benchmarks that reveal when large language models fail at reasoning tasks that seem simple to people. In 2022 she was named a MacArthur Fellow for this work and became an ACL Fellow the same year. She has since moved to Stanford University, where she holds the Dieter Schwarz Foundation Professorship in Computer Science and is a Senior Fellow at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI, continuing work on democratizing generative AI through smaller models and on pluralistic alignment of AI systems with diverse human values.
people.name: Yejin Choi
people.moniker: Dieter Schwarz Foundation Professor, Stanford University

people.hook: Yoshua Bengio has spent his career pushing neural networks from a marginal idea into the foundation of modern AI, and more recently has turned much of his attention to the risks that AI now poses. Born in Paris and raised in Canada, he earned a PhD in computer science from McGill University before joining the Universite de Montreal, where he has been a professor since the early 1990s. His 2003 paper A Neural Probabilistic Language Model helped establish the use of learned word representations in language modeling, an idea that became central to later large language models, and in 2014 he co-authored the paper introducing generative adversarial networks with Ian Goodfellow and others. He founded Mila, the Quebec Artificial Intelligence Institute, building it into one of the world's largest academic centers for deep learning research, and in 2016 co-founded the AI startup Element AI. In 2018 he shared the ACM A.M. Turing Award with Yann LeCun and Geoffrey Hinton for his contributions to deep learning. In recent years he has chaired the International AI Safety Report and, in June 2025, launched LawZero, a nonprofit research organization focused on building safe, non-agentic AI systems.
people.name: Yoshua Bengio
people.moniker: Professor, Universite de Montreal, and founder of Mila and LawZero
